For example, leveraging aligned embeddings from adversarial training or bilingual word vectors can provide a strong initial signal. Additionally, monolingual word counts and co-occurrence statistics in each language can be used to regularize and disambiguate noisy or ambiguous entries in the matrix. By combining these signals within a matrix completion setup, our framework effectively mitigates the shortcomings of any single source of information and learns translation mappings that are robust and discriminative even in the face of incomplete or noisy data. To ensure scalability and generalizability, our method is designed to be both   effective   and   extendable  , supporting easy incorporation of new features or data sources. The performance of our approach is evaluated across a wide range of language pairs, including both high-resource and low-resource settings. Experiments show that our model achieves   state-of-the-art results   in terms of precision and recall of predicted translations, outperforming existing methods that rely on similar or more constrained assumptions.

The task of machine reading comprehension (MRC) has seen remarkable progress over the past decade. Initially, MRC models were primarily evaluated on structured and curated datasets such as SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) and CoQA (Khashabi et al., 2018), in which questions are posed based on single passages of carefully written text. These problems are often well-posed, with a single correct answer that is typically a short span from the passage. However, in real-world environments, the landscape is significantly richer and more complex. Questions from online users are often posed independently of well-defined source documents and may require synthesizing information from multiple relevant sources. These sources are typically real-world web documents retrieved from search results that may be lengthy, unstructured, and semantically diverse. Moreover, questions in this domain range from factual queries to more open-ended questions about the reasons for an event, the procedure for an activity, or even the opinion of an entity. This paper addresses the challenge of real-world MRC, where not only is the passage context unstructured and potentially multi-source, but the answers themselves may be multifaceted, with multiple valid responses to a single question. This variability originates not only from the ambiguity and plurality of human expression but also from the presence of duplicate or overlapping information across web documents. These characteristics impose new demands on MRC systems, requiring them to (1) support the identification of multiple correct answers, (2) manage multiple occurrences of the same or similar answers across contexts, and (3) integrate the context coherently when synthesizing information from multiple retrieval results. To address these challenges, we propose a   multi-answer, multi-task framework   for real-world MRC. In our approach, we treat each reference answer as a separate output task, enabling us to model the variation in the severity and quality of answers. To account for the possibility of multiple occurrences of the same answer within the context, we employ   minimum risk training (MRT)   techniques to bias the model toward more robust answers based on expected risk minimization. In addition, to manage the complexity of very long or concatenated context strings, we implement a   simple heuristic passage extraction strategy   to extract the most relevant segments from the input, improving both performance and efficiency. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we apply our model to the DuReader dataset (He et al., 2018), a challenging real-world MRC benchmark derived from Baidu’s search logs.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled impressive progress in the task of text summarization, particularly in generating abstractive summaries that go beyond merely extracting existing sentences from the input. This capability becomes especially crucial when dealing with opinionated texts, such as product reviews, social media posts, and argumentative essays, where the goal is to capture the  essence  of the content while preserving the subjective nuance and reasoning of the original text. A successful abstractive summarizer for opinions and arguments must not only distill key information into a concise summary but also maintain the clarity, fluency, and coherence required to convey complex ideas accurately. Previous approaches to abstractive summarization have primarily relied on rule-based systems, template-based methods, or pointer-generator models that combine extraction and abstraction (See et al., 2017). While these models are effective for news articles and other general-domain texts, they often fall short in capturing the subtle interplay of opinions, arguments, and counter-arguments present in opinionated texts. This challenge is compounded by the need to generalize across diverse types of content and effectively prune irrelevant or redundant information that may hinder the clarity of the final summary. In this work, we propose a novel attention-based neural network model designed specifically for abstractive summarization of opinionated text. Our model leverages a hierarchical encoder-decoder architecture enhanced with a learnable importance-based sampling mechanism, which allows the encoder to focus on the most salient segments of the input text. This selective attention mechanism is essential for efficiently encoding the critical opinions, arguments, and justifications present in the input while reducing noise from surrounding content. By explicitly modeling the importance of different text segments, the model is better able to preserve the central thesis and structure of the original document in the summary. The decoder, on the other hand, generates the summary using a sequence of attention-guided steps. At each decoding step, it draws context not only from the previous decoding step but also from the most relevant parts of the input text, enabling the model to generates paraphrased content that reflects the core meaning of the input while avoiding direct copying of full sentences. This dual-process mechanism ensures that the final summary is not only concise and informative but also grammatically correct and fluent. To evaluate our model, we construct two new datasets comprising movie reviews and arguments, focusing on source material that is inherently opinionated and structured in a way that challenges conventional summarization systems.

Machine translation (MT) has traditionally relied on the atomic unit of "words" as the building blocks for modeling the relationship between source and target languages. This reliance often necessitates word segmentation, part-of-speech tagging, and external lexical resources, which may not be readily available or accurate for all language pairs — particularly those lacking substantial annotated resources or having highly morphological, agglutinative, or orthographically inconsistent structures. In this paper, we explore an alternative paradigm by entirely dispensing with the notion of words and modeling translation directly between character strings. This approach presents a fresh perspective on MT as a problem of transformation between raw character sequences, underpinned by the premise that robust translation does not necessarily require tokenization or static vocabulary definitions, and can instead emerge from sequence-level alignment and rewriting patterns. Our core contribution is the introduction of a character-based machine translation framework grounded in phrasal inversion transduction grammar (ITG) alignment techniques, which traditionally operate at the word or phrase level. We apply these alignment methodologies at the character substring level, treating sequences of characters as units for both source and target languages. This allows us to train a character-based translation model using substring alignments, which are akin to word or phrase alignments in traditional MT, yet are unbounded by predefined vocabulary. The resulting model is embedded within a phrase-based MT framework, enabling it to leverage the strengths of structured translation while eliminating the need for any prior linguistic segmentation. To facilitate effective and efficient substring alignment, we introduce two key innovations: a look-ahead parsing algorithm and substring-informed prior probabilities. The look-ahead parser anticipates potential alignment paths in the target character sequence to avoid myopic local decisions, enhancing the model's ability to capture longer-range structural relationships. Meanwhile, substring-informed priors guide the alignment process by leveraging the frequency and co-occurrence statistics of character substrings across the training data, thereby augmenting the model’s inductive biases and reducing ambiguity in alignment learning. Our evaluation across multiple language pairs demonstrates that this character-based system achieves performance levels comparable to contemporary word-based approaches while substantially improving the handling of unknown or rare words. This is a particularly significant advantage in scenarios with limited training data or for language pairs with rich morphology or non-standard orthographies. By eliminating the dependency on word-level segmentation and leveraging a more fine-grained alignment strategy, the proposed model represents a scalable and versatile approach to machine translation that transcends the limitations of traditional lexical boundaries.

The annotation of discourse structures is a crucial step in advancing natural language processing (NLP) systems toward a deeper understanding of real-world language phenomena. Discourse relations—such as elaboration, contrast, cause, and result—serve as a bridge between surface syntactic structures and coherent, interpretable meaning at the text level. Over the past two decades, the development of discourse-annotated corpora such as the Penn Discourse Treebank (Prasad et al., 2008) and the RST Discourse Treebank (Carlson et al., 2001) has significantly contributed to research in discourse parsing and reasoning. However, these gold-standard corpora are mostly limited in size due to the high cost and complexity associated with capturing detailed discourse annotations that require deep linguistic knowledge and consistent inter-annotator agreement. The barriers to large-scale discourse annotation are twofold: (1) the sheer complexity of capturing discourse phenomena, which often requires contextual reasoning and domain expertise, and (2) the prohibitive cost and time required to annotate text using traditional methods involving trained linguists or experts. These challenges have limited the availability of discourse resources—especially for under-resourced languages—hampering progress in building robust discourse-aware NLP systems. While crowdsourcing has emerged as a scalable and cost-effective method for generating linguistically rich corpora in task domains such as syntactic parsing and semantic role labeling, the same has not been achieved for discourse annotation until now. In this paper, we propose a novel two-stage crowdsourcing approach to efficiently and cost-effectively develop a discourse-annotated corpus at scale. Our method decomposes the discourse annotation task into two distinct but interdependent subtasks: (1) discourse segmentation, and (2) discourse relation labeling. By decoupling the coarse-grained segmentation of discourse units (e.g., units such as clauses or sentences that function together in a discourse structure) from the fine-grained labeling of connections between these units, we significantly reduce both the cognitive load on workers and the required expertise for annotation. Each worker task is designed to focus on a well-defined minimal linguistic decision, thus enabling us to maintain high-quality annotations even under time constraints. Our approach is evaluated in the context of building a 30,000-sentence discourse-annotated corpus in Japanese, a language that has been relatively underrepresented in discourse resources. The entire annotation process, spanning both stages, is conducted within less than eight hours using a carefully designed annotation interface, making this the fastest recorded effort of its kind to date.

事件抽取是信息抽取领域的重要研究方向之一，旨在从自然语言文本中识别并抽取事件触发词及其相关的论元。在英文事件抽取领域，已有大量研究取得了显著成果，尤其是在利用特征工程和机器学习方法建模事件类型、触发词与论元的关系等方面。然而，与英文相比，中文事件抽取的研究相对较少，其研究仍处于初步阶段。中文语言自身的特点，例如字词边界模糊、语法规则灵活、多义性强等，使得中文事件抽取面临独特挑战。 Li 等人（2012）提出了基于流水线（pipeline）架构的事件抽取系统，在英文事件抽取中取得了较好的效果。然而，这一流水线式方法存在明显的误差传播问题：其早期模块（如触发词识别）中的错误将直接影响后续模块（如实体、论元识别）的表现。此外，该系统在特征设计方面较为简单，偏向于句法层面的特征，缺乏对语言多层结构的充分建模，这在中文数据中尤为明显。 本文提出了一种基于联合建模（joint modeling）与丰富语言学特征的中文事件抽取模型，旨在从多个语言学层面捕捉事件结构的细微信息，同时缓解流水线系统的误差传播问题。我们的主要贡献如下： 首先，我们采用联合建模方式，将事件触发词识别与论元识别耦合为一个统一的目标函数进行学习，而非采用传统的模块化流水线架构。这种联立优化的方式能够更好地利用事件结构中的共现信息，从而提升模型鲁棒性与数据利用效率。 其次，我们引入了多层次的丰富语言学特征，涵盖了字、词、句乃至篇章层面的结构特征。在字符层面，我们利用中文特有的字形和字义特征，建模识别触发词与论元的潜在关系。在词汇层面，我们结合词性、词义、以及实体类别的信息，以提升事件抽取的准确性。在句法层面，我们引入依赖关系特征，以捕捉句子结构对事件要素的约束。在篇章层面，则使用上下文语义和句间连贯性特征，为跨句子的事件识别提供语义线索。 我们的实验在ACE 2005数据集上进行，并针对中文子集进行了评估。实验结果表明，与Li等人的流水线系统相比，我们的联合建模与多层语言学特征相结合的方法在事件抽取的各项指标上均有显著提升，包括F1值和召回率。尤其在论元识别任务中，结合语义一致性建模的联合框架显示出明显优势，验证了联合建模策略在中文事件抽取中的有效性。 综上所述，本文提出的基于联合建模与多语言学特征的模型为中文事件抽取提供了一种新的研究方向，有效克服了现有系统在结构建模和语义融合方面的不足。未来的研究期望进一步探索基于深度神经网络的自动化建模方式，并将事件抽取应用于更广泛的实际任务中，如新闻摘要、知识图谱构建等。重建一些全新的语言学模型与任务优化目标，也仍是这一领域的重要发展方向。 解释以下对话中AI助手的部分： assistant In this conversation, the AI assistant acts as a research writer or collaborator who generates the   introduction   section of an academic paper in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP), particularly focusing on Event Extraction and Chinese information extraction. Active learning techniques have emerged as a powerful tool for reducing annotation effort in machine learning, particularly in the context of high-dimensional or costly datasets. Traditionally, active learning systems query users for labels on individual instances, typically selecting those where the model's uncertainty is highest. This has proven effective in scenarios where instance labeling is the bottleneck. However, in many real-world settings, especially in structured prediction tasks like sequence labeling, the annotation process is not atomic with respect to instances; instead, users or domain experts naturally provide feedback on features or substructures within instances—for example, labeling a particular part of speech tag or entity type in a sentence, or annotating a specific morphological feature of a word. Given this natural alignment between user knowledge and the model’s feature space, we propose an alternative paradigm of active learning:   active learning by labeling features  . Unlike traditional methods where the learner solicits labels on full instances, in our framework, the machine asks for   direct feedback on specific features  , such as whether a tag agreement feature should be true or false in a given context, or the correctness of a particular part-of-speech tag in a phrase. This approach directly leverages prior information about the feature space, akin to generalized expectation (GE) learning, where a model is trained to minimize the discrepancy between expected and target feature values derived from unlabeled data. Indeed, our method builds upon GE by replacing the assumption of a fixed prior with an adaptive, iterative process in which the model actively selects features to label. This not only enables the use of large volumes of unlabeled data but also allows the model to focus on the features which are most informative for resolving its current state of uncertainty. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in simulated and real user studies on two sequence labeling tasks: named entity recognition (NER) and part-of-speech (POS) tagging. Our experiments show that labeling features directly leads to models that outperform both passive learning with features and traditional instance-based active learning. This is attributed to the more efficient usage of annotation effort, as the model avoids querying for full instance labels, which can be redundant or ambiguous. Furthermore, preliminary interface experiments suggest that tools designed to solicit multiple feature annotations in a single user interaction—such as interfaces that highlight multiple tags or relationships within a sentence—can further increase the annotation speed and the quality of the received labels.

Grammar is a fundamental aspect of language comprehension, and grammatical correctness has long been a significant concern in educational, professional, and computational language processing settings. Over the past decade, the field of Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) has seen substantial progress, with traditional statistical machine translation (SMT) systems achieving remarkable performance on standard benchmarks. However, the advent of neural sequence-to-sequence models (NMT) brought about an expected shift in the approach to GEC, with hopes that their ability to encode complex sentence structures and leverage end-to-end learning would yield state-of-the-art results. Surprisingly, initial attempts using neural methods in GEC fell short of the prior SMT baselines, resulting in a stagnation in the adoption of neural techniques for this task. This disparity between NMT's widespread success in translation and its initial underperformance in GEC has sparked new lines of inquiry, and our work is motivated by a compelling hypothesis:  the problem of grammatical error correction, particularly in low-resource settings, shares significant similarities with the low-resource machine translation task . In both settings, the models must learn to map a source sentence to a grammatically or semantically correct variant, often under data scarcity and with limited access to annotated or parallel corpora. By drawing this parallel, we aim to bridge the gap between GEC and low-resource machine translation, leveraging the extensive body of research and methodological innovations in the latter domain and applying these to the GEC task. In this paper, we explore how techniques originally developed for low-resource machine translation can be effectively adapted to the field of grammatical error correction. We demonstrate that incorporating strategies such as source-side noise addition, domain-adaptation techniques, customized training objectives tailored to the unique requirements of GEC, and transfer learning using monolingual data significantly boosts performance. Importantly, these methods are model-agnostic and can be integrated into various GEC frameworks regardless of their architectural specifics. To ensure robust and reliable evaluation, we establish a set of guidelines for conducting reproducible and trustworthy experiments in neural GEC. Empirically, our proposed approach outperforms the previously state-of-the-art neural GEC systems by more than 10% in M² score on the CoNLL-2014 benchmark and by 5.9% on the JFLEG test set. Furthermore, we observe that our best models also surpass the best non-neural systems on both benchmarks, achieving over 2% and 4% improvements in M² score on CoNLL-2014 and JFLEG, respectively.

Recent years have witnessed increasing interest in relation extraction (RE), which aims to identify semantic relations between entities from unstructured text. Traditionally, relation extraction has been often performed after a prior phase of entity extraction, where specific entities in a text are first identified before determining the relationships they have with one another. While this pipelined approach has achieved considerable success and has been the dominant method for research and applications, it treats entity and relation recognition as separate tasks with no direct interaction during training or inference. This separation, although computationally convenient, inherently limits the model's ability to exploit the rich and intricate dependencies and interactions that exist between entity and relation decision boundaries. To address these limitations, researchers have proposed  joint  methods for learning entity and relation extraction tasks simultaneously. These approaches are well-motivated by the fact that entities and their relations are fundamentally interdependent, and modeling them together offers a richer learning and inference mechanism. A variety of joint models have been introduced, including pipeline-based architectures incorporated with feedback loops, and deep neural networks with shared representations in which input text is simultaneously processed by both entity and relation modules. These methods leverage the mutual dependencies to improve accuracy and robustness over the pipelined approaches, particularly in handling ambiguity and partial observations. Despite the advantages of joint modeling, current approaches often involve complex model structures, which can require significant computational resources and careful design of shared layers. Moreover, the optimization of joint models is non-trivial, because the loss functions used are often local and do not fully encode the global structure of the joint task. This can result in suboptimal solutions where errors at the entity recognition stage are propagated to relation extraction, leading to cascading performance degradation. To overcome these challenges, we propose a   joint minimum risk training (J-MRT)   approach for entity and relation extraction. Instead of treating entity detection and relation classification as decoupled problems, our model is trained to jointly minimize a global risk function that considers the impact of joint predictions over the entire output space. This allows the system to capture dependencies between entity and relation decisions in an end-to-end fashion. The global loss encourages the model to infer both components consistently and accurately, which is crucial for achieving performance gains in tasks involving long-distance dependencies and interdependent decisions. Minimum risk training has been widely adopted in tasks like sequence labeling and structured prediction, where the model's objective is to reduce the overall risk or expected loss over the predicted structure.

The ability to infer the meaning of a new word from a small number of utterances is a hallmark of human language acquisition. Even first-time listeners, particularly children, can often deduce the broad semantic scope of an unfamiliar word by analyzing a handful of contexts. Distributional Semantic Models (DSMs), on the other hand, typically require extensive co-occurrence statistics to build meaningful representations. These models rely on the distributional hypothesis — that words with similar meaning tend to appear in similar contexts — but this hypothesis loses efficacy when data is sparse. This limitation becomes increasingly problematic in practical NLP settings where the vocabulary demand is vast and out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words are commonplace, especially in low-resource domains. Addressing this challenge is crucial not only for robust language understanding but also for developing systems that emulate human-like learning efficiency. Recent advances in few-shot learning have shed light on techniques to handle sparse data in areas such as computer vision and general sequence modeling, yet such methods have seen comparatively limited application in the domain of continuous word representations. In this paper, we propose Mem2Vec, a novel memory-based method for few-shot word representation learning. Inspired by memory augmentation and retrieval mechanisms, Mem2Vec operates on the idea that distributions of pre-existing word representations can act as a form of "long-term memory" to guide accurate estimates of new or rarely-seen words. By effectively leveraging semantic similarity between known and unknown words, Mem2Vec does not simply rely on the local context of an unfamiliar word to construct its representation, but instead engages the surrounding language space as an implicit, distributed form of prior knowledge. Our method is built upon a pre-trained embedding space and introduces a mechanism to modulate representations in a computationally efficient and linguistically aware manner. The core innovation lies in the integration of a dynamic, interactive retrieval process with the embedding architecture, allowing the model to query the memory of common semantic roles and syntactic patterns. This interaction is governed by similarity and analogical reasoning, making Mem2Vec particularly favorable for low-resource settings. To evaluate the effectiveness of Mem2Vec, we conduct comprehensive experiments on two challenging few-shot word similarity tasks, where the model is required to generalize from minimal context windows. We also measure the utility of the produced embeddings in downstream tasks, specifically with Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Sentiment Classification, using established baselines as points of comparison.

Constituency parsing is a core task in natural language processing, aiming to uncover hierarchical structure in sentences. While Continuous Constituency Parsing has been widely studied and successfully applied, Discontinuous Constituency Parsing (DCP) remains a challenging and less developed area. Discontinuous phrase structures are common in languages with flexible word order (such as German, Swedish, and Czech) and are also present in syntactic phenomena like scrambling and pied-piping. A transition-based approach is often employed in DCP due to its efficiency; however, it faces a critical limitation: the decision at any given step may depend on information embedded in distant or previously hidden parts of the configuration, such as the stack or the buffer. Traditional models, such as the structured perceptron, aggregate features from local state components, potentially missing long-range dependencies and global contextual information. This bottleneck significantly hampers their performance on discontinuous structures. In this paper, we present a novel neural architecture for Discontinuous Constituency Parsing designed to overcome this limitation. Our key insight is to replace the traditional feature-based model with a recursive neural network that maintains a global configuration representation. By encoding the entire state—composed of the stack, the buffer, and the partially built parse tree—into a unified vector representation, our model allows for long-range interactions between different components of the parsing configuration. This ensures that, regardless of how far apart elements are in the stack or the buffer, their influence can still be captured during decision-making. We provide a comprehensive methodology for building the global configuration representation by recursive aggregation of sub-representations for individual elements such as words, full constituent trees, and stack states. This approach is not only flexible but also semantically meaningful, as it allows different component interactions to be learned through non-linear transformations in the hidden layers of the neural model. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of different types of   swap oracles  —the procedures used to annotate correct transition sequences for training data—on the model's performance. We analyze how oracle design affects the learning process and the types of discontinuous structures that are more susceptible to errors. This investigation helps us understand where the strengths and weaknesses of our model lie, and how oracle design can be optimized for accurate training. Our contributions are as follows: (1) the first end-to-end neural model for Discontinuous Constituency Parsing, capable of maintaining a global view of the parsing configuration; (2) a detailed framework for building global representations by recursively aggregating sub-components; and (3) extensive empirical analysis of the model's behavior under different oracle setups and performance evaluation on benchmark datasets.

The automated identification of text polarity—determining whether a word or phrase expresses a positive or negative sentiment—is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP). Its applications span across various domains, including text classification, spam filtering, product review analysis, survey response analysis, and the study of online discussions and social media sentiment. Accurate sentiment analysis hinges on the ability to understand the inherent polarity of words within the context of their usage. This is a challenging problem due to the vast number of words in human language, their polysemy, and the subtle ways in which they can express sentiment. Hence, developing methods that can efficiently and accurately assign polarity signs to words remains a crucial goal in NLP. Traditional methods for polarity identification rely on manually annotated lexicons, such as SentiWordNet or subjective lexicons derived from crowdsourcing. However, these resources are limited in size, domain, and coverage, and often require heavy human intervention for maintenance and extension. To overcome these limitations, recent approaches have turned to machine learning and graph-based models that exploit distributional semantics. These methods leverage the idea that the meaning of a word is closely related to the words that appear in its context, often forming densely connected semantic networks known as word co-occurrence or relatedness graphs. In this paper, we present a novel approach to identifying the polarity of words using a Markov random walk model over a large word relatedness graph. Our method operates by performing a probabilistic traversal through the graph, where the positions and transitions are influenced by the known polarity labels of a subset of words—represented as seed nodes. Starting from a given word, the random walk simulates a process of semantic diffusion, where the influence of each labeled node spreads across the network. The final stationary distribution of the walk assigns a polarity estimate (both in sign and magnitude) to any word in the graph. A major advantage of our approach is its generality and flexibility. The model supports two key operational settings: (i) a semi-supervised setting, where a reasonably large set of labeled words (positive and negative) is used to refine the effectiveness of the model, and (ii) an unsupervised setting, where only a small set of highly confident seed words is provided to initialize the process. In the semi-supervised case, the model benefits from the extra supervision, allowing for faster convergence and more accurate polarity estimates.

The ability to accurately represent the meaning of a sentence in a continuous vector space is a significant milestone toward building robust and effective natural language understanding systems. Vector space models (VSMs) have proven to be powerful for capturing semantic relationships between words and, more recently, phrases and sentences (Mikolov et al., 2013; Socher et al., 2012). However, one of the major challenges in this line of research is modeling  compositional semantics , that is, how the meaning of a sentence is constructed from the meanings of its constituent parts. While early compositional models incorporated word order and grammatical structure to some extent, they often treated these syntactic cues as flexible or static rules rather than as first-class participants in the semantic composition itself. In recent years, there has been significant interest in integrating syntactic structure into the representation of meaning, motivated by the intuition that the hierarchical structure of language plays a critical role in how meaning is composed. Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) offers a particularly attractive approach to this problem due to its transparent mapping between syntactic structure and combinatory operations directly defined over semantic representations (Steedman, 2000). This short yet expressive rule-based formalism allows for the composition of semantic representations in a compositionally accurate and linguistically grounded way. This paper introduces   Combinatory Categorial Autoencoders (CCG Autoencoders)  , a novel model that combines the syntactic combinatorial structure of CCG with the representational power of neural networks to learn distributed sentence embeddings. The model uses CCG combinators not merely as a parse tree structure but as a guide for meaningful transformations of vector representations. Each combinator is responsible for non-linearly combining the vector representations of its constituents in a way that aligns with the type-shifting rules of the grammar, thereby enforcing consistency between syntactic form and semantic function. A key contribution of the model is its unification of discrete syntactic rules with differentiable operations, enabling the end-to-end learning of sentence representations that are both interpretable and accurate. The CCG Autoencoder is trained to reconstruct input sentences from compositional vector representations while being guided by the grammatical structure of CCG derivations. This explicitly couples composition and inference, offering the potential to scale compositional modeling techniques beyond shallow structures toward truly syntactically-structure sensitive semantics. We evaluate the proposed model on a range of semantic tasks, including paraphrase detection, textual entailment, and sentence similarity, and demonstrate that integrating explicit syntactic structure significantly enhances performance compared to syntax-agnostic baselines.

Semantic parsing is a core problem in natural language processing, aiming to convert a natural language sentence into a formal meaning representation such as a first-order logic formula or a database query. This has enabled applications in question answering, dialogue systems, and programming by demonstrating systems that can process and understand the meaning of spoken or written language. However, one particularly challenging variant of semantic parsing is the setting where training data consists   only of denotations  —the final output of the semantic representation, such as the correct answer to a question—without access to the   intermediate semantic parses  . This scenario, known as semantic parsing from denotations or  denotation-guided semantic parsing , is of great practical importance because denotations (e.g., factual answers) are often readily available in large quantities via knowledge bases, web crawls, or crowdsourcing, while explicitly annotated semantic representations are not. Despite this, the problem has only gained significant traction in recent years due to the challenges it poses in model training and learning. The lack of explicit semantic supervision in this setting presents two key challenges. First, without access to the correct parse during training, the model must directly explore the vast and often highly combinatorial space of possible semantic parses, using only the final denotation to inform credit assignment. Second, since the learning objectives in this setting are inherently indirect and approximate, choosing the best way to update the model's parameters becomes a critical challenge, as naively applying traditional parsing strategies often leads to poor convergence or suboptimal performance. To tackle these challenges, this paper proposes a novel framework for semantic parsing from denotations. First, we introduce the concept of   policy shaping  —a technique inspired by reinforcement learning—to guide the search over possible semantic parses toward those that are more linguistically plausible and grounded in the input text. By influencing the policy used to generate candidate parses, we can provide stronger and more reliable supervision signals for learning, even in the absence of explicit parses. Second, we derive a   generalized update equation   that unifies and extends the parameter update strategies used across three major families of learning algorithms (gradient-based, reinforcement learning, and structured prediction methods), enabling accurate and efficient training in a unified mathematical framework. We evaluate our framework on a recently introduced dataset for sequential question answering, a challenging domain that involves multiple steps of reasoning. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves a new state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing methods by 5.0% in exact match accuracy.

Sentence simplification is a key task in natural language processing (NLP) that aims to transform complex sentences into simpler, more accessible versions while preserving the essential meaning. This task is particularly important for improving readability in educational settings, aiding individuals with cognitive or linguistic impairments, and enhancing the effectiveness of multilingual and cross-lingual systems. Traditionally, sentence simplification has been approached with statistical and rule-based models, often involving post-editing or a simplification transcription from experts. With the rise of data-driven methods, especially in machine translation and sequence-to-sequence architectures, neural models have become the dominant approach for sentence simplification. These models often learn to perform simplification without explicit rule-based guidance, relying instead on large-scale parallel corpora of complex–simple sentence pairs. Recently, advancements in neural network architecture, particularly the Transformer model, have enabled substantial improvements in the representation of linguistic information through self-attention mechanisms. These models can capture both local and global dependencies within a sentence, making them well-suited to the task of simplification. However, despite their success, fully data-driven approaches can struggle with certain aspects of simplification, such as handling domain-specific vocabulary, enforcing syntactic constraints, or preserving consistent lexical choices across distributions of test data. In this paper, we propose a novel method that integrates a Transformer-based neural architecture with an external paraphrase knowledge base specifically designed for sentence simplification: the Simple PPDB (Paraphrase Database for Simplification). This integration introduces two key innovations: (1) the incorporation of dynamic rule adaptation, where the model selectively applies simplification patterns from the Simple PPDB during decoding, and (2) the use of static rule encoding, where paraphrase-based simplification rules are preprocessed and encoded into the model’s input representation to guide the overall simplification process. By combining the strengths of Transformer-based architecture with domain-specific linguistic rules, we aim to improve the accuracy and fluency of simplified outputs. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed integrated model not only outperforms existing state-of-the-art models for sentence simplification on standard benchmark datasets but also shows superior performance in utilizing simplification rules effectively. We conduct detailed analyses to evaluate how the model interacts with paraphrase knowledge, such as which types of rules are most frequently applied and their impact on surface and semantic simplification. These findings highlight the potential of synergistically combining learning-based models and rule-based resources for improving structured language generation tasks.

Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved the performance of sequence tagging tasks such as named entity recognition (NER), part-of-speech (POS) tagging, and chunking. Among these, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and their variants have become the state-of-the-art in modeling sequential data due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies and model contextual information effectively. Despite the widespread use of LSTM-based models in various NLP applications, a critical challenge remains underappreciated in the community: the non-deterministic nature of these models and the variability caused by different random initialization seeds and hyperparameter settings. While prior studies often focus on optimizing individual hyperparameters or model architectures, they typically report a single evaluation metric (e.g., F1-score) across a set of configurations, implicitly assuming that results are reproducible and statistically stable. However, the increasing complexity of neural network models and the inherent sensitivity of their training to random seeds and other stochastic processes call into question the robustness of such comparisons. This paper addresses this critical issue by analyzing the performance variability of LSTM networks across multiple randomly initialized runs for five common sequence tagging tasks. We argue that relying on a single performance score—often reported as the highest or average of two or three runs—can be misleading and leads to an incomplete understanding of a model’s behavior. Instead, we advocate for a more comprehensive evaluation methodology that includes the comparison of score distributions across multiple executions. Our empirical analysis is based on the evaluation of 50,000 trained LSTM networks, where each configuration is initialized with a unique random seed. Our results reveal that seemingly identical models—configured with the same hyperparameters and training data—can exhibit statistically significant variations in performance, with a maximum observed difference of one full percentage point in F1-score in the case of two NER systems. This variation is not trivial: the difference can flip the perception of a model from being state-of-the-art to mediocre. We highlight the implications of this variability by comparing two recent NER systems. For each system, we show how performance can drastically change based on the random seed used during training, a factor that is typically disregarded in prior work. Moreover, our experimental results identify LSTM network architectures that not only achieve superior performance but also demonstrate high stability across random seed variations and other hyperparameters such as learning rates and dropout values.

Semi-supervised learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for natural language processing (NLP) tasks, particularly in domain adaptation settings where labeled data in the target domain is limited or nonexistent. In traditional supervised learning, the performance of a model is highly dependent on the availability of large, high-quality labeled datasets. However, in many real-world applications, especially in specialized domains such as medical text processing, finance, or legal documents, collecting labeled data is a costly and time-consuming task. Unsupervised representation learning has been widely used to leverage large volumes of unlabeled data to generate augmenting features that can improve model performance. While effective in certain scenarios, unsupervised methods often lack the ability to incorporate task-relevant signals, which are critical for achieving high performance on downstream NLP tasks. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a dynamic dependency network model for semi-supervised representation learning. Our proposed model combines the strengths of semi-supervised learning by making use of both labeled data from a source domain and unlabeled data from both the source and target domains. The core idea is to construct a task-specific dynamic dependency network that can effectively encode the statistical dependencies and semantic structure of the input data, while being guided by the limited labeled information in the source domain. A key contribution of this work is the design of a flexible and scalable network architecture that dynamically adjusts to the task requirements and data distributions. The model learns task-informative representations by iteratively refining the structure and parameters of the dependency network using pseudo-labels generated from the unlabeled target domain data. By doing so, the learned representations are better aligned with the target task, enabling improved generalization even in the absence of labeled examples in the target domain. We evaluate the proposed method on two fundamental NLP tasks: part-of-speech (POS) tagging and syntactic chunking. For the POS tagging experiments, the source domain data is drawn from the widely used Wall Street Journal (WSJ) corpus, and the target domain is the MEDLINE biomedical corpus. For syntactic chunking, we use WSJ as the source domain and the Brown corpus as the target. Our experiments demonstrate that the dynamic dependency network significantly outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised representation learning methods in both tasks. These results suggest that integrating limited labeled data with abundant unlabeled data through a well-designed semi-supervised framework can lead to more effective and adaptable features for domain-specific NLP applications.

Semantic parsing is a key task in natural language processing that aims to convert a natural language sentence into a structured meaning representation, enabling downstream applications such as database querying, dialog systems, and question answering. Over the years, semantic parsing has attracted significant research attention due to its importance in bridging the gap between human language and machine-understandable logic or knowledge-based structures. Conventional semantic parsing systems typically follow two main components: (1) grammatical analysis or syntactic transcription of the input sentence, and (2) translation of this syntactic structure into a semantic representation. However, such systems often rely heavily on predefined grammars or hand-crafted rules, which are expensive to develop and lack generalization to new domains. In parallel, the integration of neural networks into semantic parsing has led to a shift toward fully data-driven, end-to-end models. These models, such as the sequence-to-sequence and transition-based approaches, eliminate the need for complex rules and hand-crafted grammars by learning the mapping from input sentences to meaning representations directly from annotated data. While these models have demonstrated strong performance, especially on simpler semantic grammars, they still face significant challenges when semantic representations need to enforce complex relational structures or require tight integration with external knowledge bases. This paper introduces a novel and effective end-to-end framework for semantic parsing named   Sequence-to-Action  , which combines the strengths of semantic graph representations and deep learning models. Inspired by the recent success of action-based models in parsing and code generation, our approach treats semantic parsing as a   graph generation process  , where the input sentence is mapped to a sequence of actions that modify a semantic graph incrementally. Each action corresponds to a specific graph construction operation, such as adding a node, linking nodes with an edge, or modifying an existing structure. This formulation allows the parser to directly interact with and build rich semantic graphs that reflect the relational structure of the input sentence. The key advantage of our approach lies in   bridging the semantic and structural gap   between unstructured text and structured knowledge. Specifically, the semantic graph serves as a flexible vehicle for knowledge integration. By aligning the graph construction process with a knowledge base (e.g., a database schema or a knowledge graph), our model ensures that the resulting semantic representations are not only syntactically valid but also semantically grounded in real-world knowledge. This tight coupling makes our method highly suitable for applications requiring complex reasoning and accurate knowledge base lookup.

Community-based Question Answering (cQA) services, such as Stack Overflow, Quora, and Reddit, have become increasingly popular platforms for users to solicit and provide answers to a wide variety of topics. These platforms generate a massive amount of user-generated content, with questions often spread across different posts, making the task of retrieving relevant questions highly challenging. Two critical components in the pipeline of a cQA system are   Question Detection (QD)   and   Question Retrieval (QR)  . While QD aims to identify sentences or phrases that constitute questions, QR involves retrieving the most relevant questions relevant to a given input. The accuracy of QD directly influences the performance of QR, as it helps reduce noise and improves the precision of the retrieval process. In traditional settings, identifying questions is relatively straightforward, relying on simple linguistic features such as the presence of a question mark, interrogative words (5W1H: who, what, where, when, why, how), or syntactic patterns, such as subject-verb inversion. However, in online community content, questions are often embedded in long, informal, and conversational text, and may lack lexical or syntactic indicators that are typical of formal questions. For example, a question may be expressed through a statement with a rising intonation in written form, embedded in a complex sentence, or composed of slash-separated options without any punctuation. These factors make traditional QD methods unsuitable, and hence, the need for a more robust and adaptive model arises. This paper addresses the challenge of question detection in the context of community-based Q&A platforms by proposing a novel automated approach that leverages   salient lexical and syntactic patterns   to identify question sentences with high accuracy, specifically tailored for the informal nature of online language. Our method does not rely on the presence of a question mark or any specific interrogative cues but instead focuses on the structural and contextual peculiarities of question expressions in online discourse. The model is trained and evaluated using a real-world cQA dataset to ensure practical relevance. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing traditional baselines in terms of effectiveness in detecting question sentences across different types of content. Furthermore, incorporating the output of our QD model as a pre-processing step substantially improves the performance of the subsequent question retrieval system. This highlights the importance of accurate question detection in building efficient cQA systems. In this work, we make the following contributions: 1. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of question characteristics in online community-based Q&A platforms, uncovering unique lexical and syntactic features that distinguish genuine question sentences from other types of expressions.

Distributed word representations have emerged as a foundational component in natural language processing (NLP), enabling the modeling of semantic and syntactic relations among words and facilitating significant advancements in a wide range of NLP applications, including machine translation, text categorization, and question answering. While these representations have been extensively explored and refined for languages with well-defined word boundaries—such as English—their application to Chinese, where words are often composed of multiple characters and lack explicit segmentation cues, presents unique challenges and opportunities. Chinese characters, unlike English words, are not atomic lexical units; rather, they are morphemes or components that carry independent semantic or phonetic information. Consequently, many characters share common components that express semantic or morphological relationships, offering the potential to construct more semantically and structurally rich character embeddings. Building on this insight, we propose a novel framework for learning Chinese character embeddings that incorporate component information, which we refer to as   component-enhanced Chinese character embeddings  . These embeddings explicitly exploit the internal composition of characters to enrich their representation space and capture both semantic and structural relationships between characters. In particular, we develop two distinct component-enhanced models: one based on semantic composition and the other on a mixture of semantic and typological information. The core idea is to integrate the embeddings of the composing components (e.g., radicals or semantic components) into the character embedding generation process. This is achieved through a hierarchical architecture: at the component level, embeddings are learned for each radical or sub-character component using standard distributional methods; at the character level, the composed representations are generated by combining these component embeddings in a way that preserves and leverages their semantic relationships. Furthermore, we extend our models to a   bigram-based   formulation, which allows the integration of co-occurrence statistics between adjacent character pairs, thereby incorporating sequential context about how characters are used together in real language. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct experiments on two diverse NLP tasks:   word similarity   and   text classification  . In the word similarity task, we measure the performance of our models on benchmark datasets that require capturing semantic similarity among minimal linguistic units. In the text classification task, we assess how well our character representations transfer to downstream applications such as sentiment analysis and topic categorization. Our experiments demonstrate that the inclusion of character components significantly enhances the quality of character embeddings, leading to consistent improvements over baseline models that do not exploit component information.

The recognition and parsing of multiword expressions (MWEs) remain a challenging aspect of natural language processing. MWEs, such as phrasal verbs or idiomatic expressions, exhibit syntactic, semantic, or phonological behaviors that differ from the composition of their individual components (Beebe, 1991; Sag et al., 2002). Consequently, many parsing systems have explored the integration of MWE-specific rules or recognition mechanisms in an attempt to improve performance. In principle, such integration is attractive because MWEs introduce non-compositional phenomena that standard compositional grammars may not capture effectively. Early research demonstrated that integrating MWEs into parsing procedures can enhance accuracy when MWEs are assumed to be perfectly pre-identified (Etzioni and S魂orenson, 2004; Tenr型, 2005). In these idealized scenarios, incorporating MWE information into the grammar often results in better structural analysis, as the parser need not treat MWEs as mere sequences of words but rather as units with specific behaviors. However, many of these experiments ignore the fact that real-world language processing systems do not have access to perfectly segmented MWEs. Instead, MWE recognition is typically an error-prone process, raising the question: how much benefit can be derived from integrating multiword expression recognition and parsing in real – i.e., erroneous – scenarios? In this paper, we evaluate two discriminative strategies for integrating MWE recognition into constituency parsing under non-ideal conditions. The first strategy involves the pre-processing of input text with a state-of-the-art multiword expression recognizer, followed by parsing using a standard parser. While this approach does improve certain aspects of the parser’s output—most notably the unlabeled attachment score and the accuracy of MWE recognition—it fails to yield a statistically significant improvement in the overall F-score. We argue that incorrect MWE identification introduces detrimental noise that negatively affects the parser's global structure, thereby diminishing the potential gains. The second strategy rethinks integration by embedding multiword expressions directly into the grammar of a probabilistic parser and then refining the parser's output with a reranking mechanism that is specifically tuned to reward accurate MWE incorporation. This technique results in modest but statistically significant improvements across a range of metrics, including overall attachment accuracy, MWE-specific F-score, and overall syntactic correctness. These results suggest that MWE integration is most effective when it does not rely on pre-processing, but is instead tightly coupled with the parsing process, allowing the parser to jointly optimize for both general syntactic structure and MWE-related constraints.

Grammar is a fundamental aspect of language comprehension, and grammatical accuracy is essential for effective communication. In recent years, grammatical error correction (GEC) has become an active area of research in natural language processing (NLP), with a variety of systems developed to detect and correct the types of errors that learners of a second language make in writing. Errors in language can be broadly categorized into two classes:  global  errors involving issues in syntax, word order, and logical cohesion; and  local  errors, including problems with spelling, inflection, and orthography. While traditional GEC systems have often treated these two classes separately or with equal attention, recent advances in deep learning have enabled more holistic and nuanced approaches to learning both the macro and micro structures of language in an end-to-end fashion. Despite these advances, existing neural-based GEC systems still face significant challenges, particularly in handling local, fine-grained correction tasks such as spelling and inflection corrections, which require extremely precise mechanisms, often involving small changes to a single word or subword unit. Additionally, the non-monotonic, reordering nature of global errors necessitates flexible and context-aware decoding strategies that can handle both substitution and repositioning of segments across the sentence. In this paper, we propose a novel   Nested Attention Neural Hybrid Model   for grammatical error correction that addresses these challenges through a hybrid architecture that combines character- and word-level information. Our core innovation is the introduction of a   nested attention mechanism  , which allows the model to dynamically and hierarchically capture dependencies at both the word and subword levels. Our approach is inspired by and extends upon the success of sequence-to-sequence models with attention, particularly in tasks such as machine translation and text summarization. However, unlike these tasks, where the input and output are semantically aligned, grammatical correction requires a more nuanced alignment of erroneous tokens to their corrected counterparts. The nested attention architecture is designed to first attend to the word-level semantics while simultaneously leveraging character-level representations to correct localized, morphological errors. This dual-level representation generates more robust features for both global and local correction tasks. Furthermore, the nested alignment mechanism provides interpretability by highlighting which parts of the source sentence are being considered at each decoding step, as well as which specific characters within a word need to be altered. We evaluate our model using the standard   CoNLL-14 Shared Task   benchmark dataset, a widely adopted benchmark for GEC that includes a mix of spelling, morphological, and syntactic errors.

Pluralization is a fundamental morphological process essential in natural language generation (NLG) systems, particularly in tasks such as string interpolation in user interfaces and automated content generation. While morphological operations like pluralization are well-studied and accurately modeled in major European languages such as English and Spanish, such facilities remain largely underdeveloped for many resource-poor languages, especially those in the Bantu language family. Bantu languages are agglutinative and exhibit complex noun class systems, where number agreement affects not only nouns but also modifiers and verbs. This complexity presents a significant challenge in the automatic generation of grammatically correct plural forms. The Bantu language family, spread across sub-Saharan Africa, contains approximately 500 genetically related languages, typically grouped into Guthrie zones based on geographical and linguistic proximity. The morphological richness of these languages—from extensive noun class systems to complex agreement patterns—has made generalizable computational approaches difficult to implement. For instance, previous work on pluralization in isiZulu and Runyankore, representing different Guthrie language zones, demonstrated that while both languages benefited from a shared reliance on morpho-syntactic and semantic features, the lack of a unified framework across diverse Bantu languages hindered broader application. This paper presents a systematic investigation into the pluralization of nouns in seven Bantu languages, drawn from three distinct Guthrie zones. The aim is to assess whether a shared computational model can be developed for these languages, building on insights from isiZulu and Runyankore. One critical issue we address is the inadequacy of the traditional Meinhof (1948) noun class schema for computational applications. Based on a detailed linguistic analysis, we found that existing noun class prefixes in these languages are underdetermined and non-deterministic, making automated pluralization unstable. To address this, we redefine the 29 noun classes traditionally assumed in Bantu taxonomy into 53 distinct morphological classes, better aligned with the observable patterns in the data. Building on this revised classification, we propose a generic pluralizer based on a rule-based system extended with statistical modeling. Our model combines morphological patterns with contextual features, including syntactic dependency structures and semantic roles, to generate accurate plural forms. The pluralizer was tested across a diverse set of tasks, including coverage testing and random sampling for each of the seven languages. The experimental results showed an overall accuracy of 93% in coverage testing and 94% in random sample evaluation, outperforming previous approaches in both isiZulu and Runyankore. This performance level demonstrates the feasibility of a generalized pluralizer across Bantu languages with divergent morphological properties.

Transliteration — the process of representing a text in one script using another — is a crucial yet challenging task in natural language processing. It plays a vital role in cross-lingual applications such as information retrieval, cross-lingual named entity recognition, and multilingual systems. Classical approaches to transliteration often relied on phonetic-based models that map characters from a source language to a target one, focusing on phonetic similarity between scripts. However, a growing body of research highlights that transliteration is not purely a phonetic phenomenon but incorporates both   spelling   (orthographic) and   pronunciation   (phonetic) patterns of the source and target words. This observation is particularly relevant in script-rich and multilingual environments, such as South and Southeast Asia, and across Latin-alphabet-based languages with varying orthographic conventions. Despite the importance of transliteration, existing models often treat source information in isolation: either relying solely on phonetic transcription rules, or using character-level mapping for orthographic patterns. However, this approach neglects the rich interplay between the two modalities and fails to exploit the full potential of combining multiple representations. In this paper, we argue that effective transliteration should integrate both   spelling   and   pronunciation   features of the source and target languages. We present a novel model that performs   joint generation   of transliterations from multiple representations, including phonetic and orthographic features of the source word, and demonstrate that this strategy leads to more accurate and robust transliterations. Our model generalizes the use of multilingual knowledge by incorporating transliterations from additional source languages, which further enriches the input information. Additionally, to enhance the model's performance, we integrate   reranking   techniques and   lexicon-based features  , allowing the system to combine learned patterns with hand-crafted knowledge. Experimental evaluations on benchmark datasets show a   significant improvement   in transliteration accuracy over state-of-the-art models, demonstrating the advantages of leveraging multiple representations and the utility of joint modeling in transliteration generation. This work contributes to the development of more flexible and accurate transliteration systems that can adapt to diverse multilingual scenarios where both spelling and pronunciation are relevant, and lays the groundwork for further research into deep integration of hybrid multimodal representations in NLP systems. Our model not only improves transliteration performance but also opens new avenues for studying the interplay between orthographic and phonetic patterns in the context of cross-lingual alignment tasks. By unifying multiple representations into a single cohesive framework, we present a step forward in making transliteration a more robust and reliable component of multilingual processing pipelines.

The disambiguation of quantifier scope is one of the classic challenges in natural language semantics and has significant implications for tasks such as question answering, text understanding, and machine reading comprehension. In natural language, sentences with multiple quantified noun phrases often allow for multiple interpretations depending on the scope relationships between the quantifiers. For example, in the sentence "Every man liked some ice cream," the structure could imply that there is a single ice cream liked by every man, or that each man liked some (possibly different) ice cream. Determining the correct scope is non-trivial and often relies not only on syntactic clues but also on pragmatic knowledge about how speakers use language to convey meaning in context. Despite the importance of pragmatic knowledge in disambiguating such structures, its use in computational models has been limited due to the difficulty of automatically acquiring and representing this knowledge at scale. Pragmatic knowledge often resides in the world knowledge of human annotators, embedded in the assumptions about speaker intentions, common usage patterns, and real-world plausibility. Traditional linguistic resources, such as dictionaries and knowledge bases, are not always sufficient to capture the subtle, context-sensitive nature of pragmatic cues. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to leveraging pragmatic knowledge for the quantifier scope disambiguation task by extracting relevant patterns directly from unstructured text. We utilize an open information extraction (OIE) system to capture implicit relationships between quantified entities and their modifiers in a wide range of real-world contexts. This extracted pragmatic knowledge is then integrated into a probabilistic Markov Logic Network (MLN) model, which allows for the combination of first-order logical rules with statistical inference to model the interactions between syntactic and pragmatic signals. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, we present preliminary results from experiments in which our model outperforms baseline systems that rely solely on syntactic features. Our findings suggest that pragmatic knowledge extracted from large corpora can significantly enhance the performance of quantifier scope disambiguation, particularly in resolving ambiguities where linguistic structures are underspecified or ambiguous. This work demonstrates the feasibility and potential impact of pragmatic information extraction for NLP tasks that require deeper semantic understanding. Moreover, it opens the door to the exploration of similar approaches for other semantic disambiguation problems where pragmatic reasoning plays a critical role. By moving beyond the limitations of purely syntactic models, our method contributes to a more context-aware and goally-driven framework for natural language understanding.

The task of processing user-generated text, such as microblog posts, poses unique challenges for natural language processing (NLP) systems. Microblog data are often informal,包含 excessive noise, and violate standard linguistic conventions, making traditional NLP pipelines for tasks like word segmentation, part-of-speech (POS) tagging, and normalization suboptimal or even inapplicable. These challenges are further exacerbated by the lack of annotated resources tailored specifically for microblog data. A typical NLP pipeline processes such tasks sequentially, where the output of one module (e.g., segmentation) serves as the input to the next (e.g., POS tagging), with error propagation potentially undermining the overall performance of downstream applications. To address these issues, we propose a transition-based model that jointly performs word segmentation, POS tagging, and text normalization. By modeling these tasks simultaneously, our approach not only mitigates error propagation but also leverages the inherent dependencies between the tasks, enhancing the robustness and accuracy of each component. Most existing approaches for microblog processing rely on annotated data or pre-trained models designed for standard text, which are often not well-suited to the idiosyncratic nature of microblog data, such as abbreviations, misspellings, short forms, and ungrammatical structures. For instance, word segmentation in microblogs is complicated by overlapping segmentations and unfamiliar token forms, which traditional Chinese segmentation models trained on newswire or other formal text often fail to handle. Similarly, POS tagging on microblog data suffer from the scarcity of training examples for less common tags due to the informal and concise writing style. While some previous work has attempted to integrate segmentation and POS tagging, few have tackled the joint modeling of segmentation, POS tagging, and normalization as a unified task. In this paper, we propose a transition-based model that naturally integrates these three components by utilizing a shared state representation and a sequence of state transitions during decoding. This approach not only allows for efficient training and inference but also facilitates the use of standard text corpora, thereby overcoming the need for annotated microblog data during training. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we introduce an annotated microblog corpus specifically tailored for joint word segmentation, POS tagging, and normalization. The dataset is annotated with fine-grained word boundaries, POS tags, and normalization forms (e.g., converting "2nite" to "tonight"), providing a comprehensive benchmark for the proposed method. Experimental results on this corpus show that our joint model significantly improves segmentation accuracy compared to traditional separate models, with an error reduction of 12.02%.

The identification of a person's native language (Native Language Identification, NLI) is a key task in computational linguistics with applications ranging from authorship profiling to educational technology and forensic analysis. NLI involves determining an author’s first language based on observable patterns of language use in a text written in a second language. The field has seen significant progress over the past decade, particularly with the use of large-scale linguistic feature sets and machine learning techniques that efficiently leverage these features to build high-performance classifiers. Such feature sets often include items like lexical, syntactic, morphological, and discourse-level phenomena, which are broadly indicative of residual influence from the author's first language. One of the challenges in NLI is the inherent sparsity of linguistic feature realizations across different languages, particularly when capturing the subtle, fine-grained distinctions necessary to reliably distinguish among closely related languages or language groups. This problem is further exacerbated when the features extracted are too detailed or specific, making them harder to generalize across diverse data, and increasing the risk of overfitting or lack of robustness under varying conditions. To address this, we draw inspiration from theoretical insights in variationist sociolinguistics—particularly the notion that speakers make choices among structurally related linguistic options based on social, linguistic, and situational factors. These insights suggest that linguistic features often function in related, overlapping clusters rather than in isolation. Building on this idea, this paper introduces a label-informed feature grouping approach for supervised machine learning. The method is based on hierarchical clustering, where the clustering criterion is guided not only by the similarity of the feature behaviors themselves, but also by the extent to which these features correlate with the target class (i.e., the native language label). By grouping similar features in this way, we achieve a more compact and general representation of the data, reducing redundancy and helping alleviate sparsity issues. At the same time, the grouping provides an opportunity for a deeper qualitative analysis of linguistic patterns that are systematically associated with native language background. To illustrate the applicability and benefits of this approach, we conduct an in-depth case study focusing on features based on verb subcategorization frames. These features are particularly relevant in NLI, as syntactic preferences related to the distribution and realization of verbal structures are well-documented to correlate with first language influence. We evaluate the impact of the proposed clustering method within a standardized NLI setting, and demonstrate that the approach not only contributes to improved quantitative performance but also facilitates the interpretation of linguistic phenomena in terms of their relationship to native language influence.

Explaining the causes or effects behind a series of events described through time is a fundamental task in both natural language processing and real-time analytics. Traditionally, uncovering such causal relationships has relied on domain-specific knowledge or specific constraints over physical systems where observable interactions are quantifiable and predictable. However, as the volume of textual data describing events in real-time—ranging from news articles to social media content—continues to grow, the need for efficiently analyzing and generating causal explanations from this text becomes increasingly important. In this paper, we introduce a novel problem: given a text and corresponding time series data, generate an explanation for a time series event by (1) detecting its causal relationships and (2) constructing a logical chain between cause and effect, thereby providing a human-understandable narrative of the underlying events. Identifying the causes or effects of a time series event from unlabeled or loosely structured text presents multiple challenges. First, the text often discusses numerous entities, and discerning which are relevant to the time series' progression demands robust feature extraction and relevance modeling. Second, the temporal dynamics of these entities are not always explicitly stated in the text, necessitating methods that can infer and validate causal dependencies between them. Finally, the explanation must be interpretable and grounded in both factual and commonsense knowledge to ensure usability in decision-making contexts. To address these challenges, we propose a novel method that leverages Granger causality—a statistical concept originally used in time series forecasting—to identify the causality of features extracted from text. These features include N-grams, topics extracted using topic modeling, sentiment scores, and combinations of these. By applying Granger causality to the time series represented by these features, we identify potential causal relationships that drive the observed temporal behavior. This allows us to detect not only key events or entities but also their influencing factors across the time domain. Beyond the detection of causal features, constructing a coherent explanation requires an ordered sequence of events that are logically and causally connected. To achieve this, we integrate a symbolic knowledge base of commonsense causal relationships with a neural reasoning model. The symbolic component provides a structured representation of existing causal knowledge, while the neural model learns to infer the most likely next step in the causal chain, trained on a curated set of commonsense causal tuples. By combining the precision of symbolic knowledge with the generalization power of neural networks, our approach generates explanations that are not only linguistically fluent but also logically sound.

Predicting eye movements is a central task in computational models of reading comprehension and cognitive processing. A promising line of research uses machine learning techniques to model and predict where a reader will fixate as they read text. Such models can provide insight into cognitive mechanisms of reading and also enable applications like adaptive educational technologies or assistive tools for individuals with visual or reading impairments. While most models aim to predict gaze patterns within the same individual (i.e., for a single reader), generalization across individuals remains a challenging and underexplored problem. This is arguably due to the substantial behavioral and cognitive variability among readers—differences in prior knowledge, reading strategies, visual processing, and language skills all contribute to variability in eye movement patterns. In 2009, Nilsson and Nivre introduced a tree-based model for predicting eye movements during reading, which captured the hierarchical and nested structure of eye movement events, such as fixations and saccades. While the model achieved strong performance on individual data, the authors suggested that this approach likely hindered generalization across readers due to the non-uniform distribution of fixation patterns across individuals. As a result, they concluded that reliable cross-reader prediction with this model was not feasible. However, their conclusion left room for alternative modeling approaches that might better handle the inherent variability by either explicitly accounting for it during training or by leveraging more data from multiple readers. In this paper, we re-evaluate the problem of cross-reader eye movement prediction and explore whether the perceived limitations of tree-based models stem from their structural constraints or the lack of suitable inductive biases.
