Moreover, these techniques often struggle with the exploration-exploitation trade-off and can fail to scale effectively in complex translation scenarios. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach that avoids the reinforcement learning framework while still optimizing at the sequence level. Our method is grounded in a new differentiable training objective based on   probabilistic n-gram matching  . This objective directly encourages the model to align target-side n-grams with reference translations, effectively incentivizing the generation of sentence-level structures that are statistically consistent with human references. Unlike RL-based methods, this approach eliminates the need for sampling and provides a more stable and deterministic training procedure. In addition to our novel sequence-level training objective, we adopt a   greedy search   strategy during training that mirrors the inference phase. This ensures that the model conditions its predictions on previously generated (potentially noisy) tokens during training, bridging the gap between training and testing. This strategy is particularly effective at mitigating exposure bias, as the model learns to recover from early errors in a manner that better reflects real-world translation dynamics. We evaluate our method on the NIST Chinese-to-English translation task, a widely used benchmark for evaluating machine translation systems.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have increasingly focused on leveraging linguistic knowledge for deeper semantic understanding. Among such knowledge, inference rules—specifically entailment and paraphrase rules—play a pivotal role by enabling reasoning over textual data. These rules allow NLP systems to answer questions, perform text simplification, and uncover implicit information in large-scale text corpora. Typically, inference rules are expressed over syntactic structures (e.g., dependency or constituency parses), and applying them efficiently over such representations remains a key challenge in building scalable NLP systems. Entailment and paraphrase are two essential forms of semantic inference. While entailment captures directional relationships where one sentence logically implies another, paraphrase characterizes bi-directional equivalence between different surface forms expressing the same meaning. Effectively applying these inference patterns at scale requires not only high-quality rule acquisition but also the design of efficient algorithms for their application and composition. A naive approach of exhaustively assembling all possible inferences is generally infeasible due to combinatorial explosion. This necessitates the development of more compact, shared representations for inference, which can both reduce computational overhead and improve inference precision. In this paper, we introduce a novel data structure, the Compact Forest, tailored for efficient inference over a large set of paraphrase and entailment rules. Our contributions include a formalism for representing and applying such rules over structured syntactic representations, the development of a new packed forest-based data structure that eliminates redundant intermediate representations while preserving all relevant inferences, and an efficient inference algorithm for navigating the compact forest. The Compact Forest generalizes and improves upon traditional methods such as beam search and n-best parsing trees by explicitly encoding shared dependencies and allowing a more compact traversal over the search space. We formally prove the correctness of our algorithm and provide both theoretical complexity analysis and empirical validation on real-world NLP tasks involving paraphrase generation and entailment prediction. Our experiments demonstrate that the Compact Forest approach not only significantly reduces the runtime and memory footprint of inference procedures but also enhances the precision of rule application over current techniques. To our knowledge, this is the first work that integrates inference over a wide range of entailment and paraphrase rules into a unified, scalable framework with strong performance guarantees. The proposed method has broad applicability in systems requiring efficient semantic reasoning and opens new directions for research in structured inference in NLP. Through this work, we advance the goal of making semantic inference both more powerful and more practical for real-time and large-scale applications.

Tokenization is a critical preprocessing step for any statistical machine translation (SMT) system. However, for languages like Chinese and Korean—those without explicit word boundaries—tokenization is inherently ambiguous and error-prone. This poses a unique challenge for SMT systems that process text as sequences of words, as the choice of segmentation directly affects translation quality. Errors introduced at the tokenization stage can propagate and compound within the overall translation process, particularly when translation systems rely solely on a single "1-best" tokenization. The conventional approach is to either force a rigid tokenization prior to translation or to use tokenization lattices that capture multiple competing tokenization hypotheses as a way to mitigate the risk of segmentation errors. While tokenization lattices supply the translation system with additional coverage and robustness, they are only a partial solution. The decoding remains separate between tokenization and translation, meaning these two steps are treated in isolation despite their deep interdependence in character-based or morphologically rich languages. In this paper, we propose a novel decoding approach for machine translation that unifies tokenization and translation into a single discriminative framework. Instead of producing a fixed lexical segmentation before translation, our system receives as input a sequence of atomic units—such as characters or subwords—that can be combined into different word forms. From this input, a single joint decoder computes a tokenization for the source language alongside a translation for the target language in a cohesive, end-to-end fashion. This formulation allows the system to learn tokenization and translation features that are jointly optimized rather than treated as separate tasks. For example, the translation model can influence the decision to combine two characters into a meaningful word if it benefits the fluency or accuracy of the resulting translation. Experiments on real-world translation tasks—from Chinese to English and Korean to Chinese—demonstrate that our joint tokenization and translation model outperforms both traditional systems using 1-best tokenizations and lattice-based baselines that incorporate multiple segmentation hypotheses. Notably, as a side benefit, the joint decoder also functions as a highly effective monolingual tokenizer, achieving significant improvements over standalone Chinese tokenizers. These results underscore the importance of treating tokenization and translation as inherently interdependent tasks and suggest that such a joint framework can lead to more accurate and robust translation systems for morphologically or segmentationally challenging languages. By integrating these two tasks within a unified model, our approach not only enhances the end-to-end translation pipeline but also opens new avenues for research into other interdependent NLP tasks, particularly in low-resource or morphologically rich language settings.

Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) is an essential task in natural language understanding, aiming to identify the predicate-argument structure in a sentence, and assign semantic roles to the arguments (Pradhan et al., 2005). Traditionally, SRL systems are specifically trained on either PropBank (PB) or NomBank (NB), which annotate passive and active verb roles and nominalized verb roles respectively. However, PB and NB correspond to two distinct logical forms and thus often result in divergent labels for the same proposition. This inconsistency not only complicates downstream NLP applications like question answering or event extraction but also poses challenges in model design due to the duplicate predicates and divergent argument annotations. In order to address the issue, researchers have attempted to combine PB and NB annotations via pipeline approaches (Hershcovich et al., 2013; Li et al., 2014). These systems first train PB and NB independently and then use combination mechanisms, often leading to performance bottlenecks due to error propagation and input redundancy. An ideal solution would benefit from an integrated SRL system that effectively utilizes both PB and NB annotations directly during training and inference, thereby avoiding the problem of separate model assumptions and reducing error propagation. In this work, we present an efficient and integrated semantic dependency parsing-based SRL system that jointly learns from both PropBank and NomBank annotations for English. Rather than treating them as separate tasks, our system proposes a unified feature-based modeling approach by learning to assign semantic roles under a shared label space. To achieve this, we first introduce the notion of "assistant argument labels"—auxiliary labels inspired from both PB and NB—to enrich the argument classification space and capture the overlapping and complementary semantic roles between the two banks. Second, we develop a large-scale feature selection procedure that efficiently evaluates the relevance of a comprehensive set of feature templates, which encode syntactic, semantic, and contextual signals. Our method identifies feature sets optimal for each label type (i.e., predicates and arguments) and suppresses the processing of less informative high-dimensional features, significantly reducing computational overhead without sacrificing effectiveness. Third, the selected features are integrated into a single accurate SRL system that jointly parses all semantic roles from both banks. This paper makes three key contributions: first, a new integrated SRL architecture that unifies PropBank and NomBank via a single semantic dependency parsing setup, eliminating the need for intermediate binarization steps; second, a novel feature selection pipeline that selects the most informative feature templates based on relevance estimation, resulting in scalable and robust models; and third, an extensive evaluation on the CoNLL-2008 shared task dataset, where our system achieves performance levels that are competitive with

The task of constructing concise and informative overviews from a set of news articles is a significant challenge in the field of natural language processing. While multi-document summarization has long been studied for generating summaries that abstract content from multiple sources, the construction of   news overview articles  —which specifically aim to provide a coherent, broad-level perspective on a particular event—introduces additional nuances. Unlike standard summarization, which often emphasizes brevity and content abstraction, an overview article requires organizing information in a structured and narrative-style format, incorporating temporal flow and key stakeholder perspectives. Traditionally, such documents are crafted collaboratively by human journalists or editors, often drawing from a large corpus of news reports published over a short timespan. However, with the increasing volatility and volume of news data, especially during breaking events, automation becomes critical to ensure timely and accurate overviews. In this paper, we propose a novel task of   news synthesis  —the automated generation of overview articles from a collection of news articles covering a specific event. This task is inherently more complex than traditional multi-document summarization in that it requires not only identifying and condensing key elements from the source material but also organizing and combining them into a coherent and consistent narrative. To achieve this, we design a news synthesis system grounded in four core components: passage   segmentation  ,   ranking  ,   selection  , and   merging  . Passage segmentation partitions the input articles into semantically meaningful units, while ranking and selection identify the most relevant segments based on their factual importance and coverage. The merging step then integrates the selected segments into a well-structured overview that reflects the key developments and perspectives surrounding the event. Our method is evaluated on the   Wikinews dataset  , which contains a diverse set of real-world news events with manually curated overview articles. We compare our approach with several representative multi-document summarization systems, such as those based on extractive models and document abstraction techniques. Our results demonstrate that the proposed news synthesis pipeline outperforms existing methods on both   automatic evaluation metrics  , including ROUGE and Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation (Rouge-L), and   manual evaluation   by human annotators, who assess the coherence, coverage, and factual accuracy of the generated overviews. These results underscore the effectiveness of our approach in capturing the essential narrative of news events, as well as its potential for deployment in real-world journalistic workflows. Moreover, we conduct a qualitative analysis to understand the patterns of information retrieval and integration made by our system, uncovering the strengths and limitations of automated synthesis in high-stakes, fast-paced environments.

Idiom token classification is a crucial task in natural language processing, as it focuses on determining whether a given token—the actual appearance of a phrase in a text—is used literally or idiomatically. This distinction is important for a wide variety of downstream applications, including semantic role labeling, question answering, and text simplification. While idioms are generally defined as fixed expressions whose meanings cannot be inferred from the meanings of the individual words (Rayson and Garside, 2000), their identification and classification are far from trivial due to the ambiguity and variability of their usage across different contexts. Traditional approaches to idiom token classification have often relied on either rule-based methods, leveraging handcrafted linguistic patterns, or supervised learning models that depend on rich feature sets capturing syntactic and semantic properties of the target phrase (Baroni and Bernardi, 2014; Post and Demberg, 2016). These models often require discourse-level features and contextual information, such as surrounding sentences or paragraph-level representations, to make accurate inferences. However, such features can be problematic, as building them requires reliance on costly preprocessing modules like coreference resolution or discourse parsing, which may not always be accurate or available in low-resource scenarios. In contrast, recent advances in distributed semantic representations, particularly those based on deep learning, have opened new perspectives for this task. Distributed models offer the ability to learn meaning from large-scale linguistic data and, crucially, to represent linguistic structure and meaning in a way that can be compared and generalized across large volumes of language. This paper explores the use of Skip-Thought Vectors (Kiros et al., 2015), a sentence-level distributed representation model, for the idiom token classification task. Skip-Thought Vectors are trained to encode the meaning of a sentence about its neighboring sentences in a discourse, such that the encoder of the model learns to reconstruct a target sentence from the encoded representations of surrounding sentences. This provides a way to induce meaning in sentences independent of manual feature engineering. Our core contribution is to demonstrate that Skip-Thought Vectors capture contextual information sufficient to classify a given idiom token occurrence as either literal or idiomatic when trained on a sliding window of text as input. By doing so, our models are able to achieve performance on par with existing state-of-the-art systems (Baroni and Bernardi, 2014; Ebert et al., 2017), while using minimal external features and no discourse-based modeling.

Automatic Text Scoring (ATS) systems have emerged as a powerful and efficient alternative to traditional human marking processes in educational and linguistic assessment. These systems are particularly well-suited for standardized tests, essay scoring, and content evaluation in large-scale settings where consistent and rapid grading is essential. Traditional ATS systems rely on handcrafted features derived from linguistic patterns, grammatical structures, lexical diversity, and fluency cues (Attali and Burstein, 2006; Amini et al., 2009; Biber et al., 2004). While such systems have demonstrated promising performance, the labor-intensive process of feature engineering often limits their flexibility and domain adaptability. Furthermore, these handcrafted features typically offer limited insight into the specific aspects of the text that the model uses to justify its scoring decisions, which hinders interpretability and trust in the system. Recent advances in neural networks have opened new avenues for modeling text in a more data-driven and interpretable manner. In particular, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and their variants have demonstrated strong performance in capturing sequential context and semantic meaning in natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as machine translation, text summarization, and sentiment analysis (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997). These models learn to represent the underlying meaning of a text from raw words without requiring extensive feature engineering. Inspired by these developments, we present a novel ATS framework that leverages deep neural networks to automatically encode text meaning and predict its quality score. Our model learns word representations by directly modeling the relationship between specific words in the input and the final score, effectively identifying the key lexical components that are most predictive of quality. In addition to delivering high accuracy and robustness across different datasets, our model is designed with interpretability in mind. To address the often "black-box" nature of neural models, we introduce a novel visualization technique that highlights the most discriminative regions of the text according to the model's attention mechanism. Drawing inspiration from recent methods for visualizing neural network decisions in image recognition tasks (Zeiler and Fergus, 2014; Simonyan et al., 2013), we propose an approach to project the model’s learned word-level contributions back into the original text space, providing clear textual evidence for the model's scoring decision. This level of interpretability not only enhances the usability of the system in domains such as educational assessment but also facilitates diagnostic analysis and model refinement. Through extensive experiments on standard ATS benchmarks, we demonstrate that our model achieves competitive performance compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches while eliminating the need for manual feature engineering.

The task of predicting the ending of a story is an intriguing and important challenge in natural language processing (NLP), as it requires deep comprehension of narratives and the ability to infer logical and coherent conclusions. This capability has broad applications in areas such as automated story generation, reading comprehension systems, and educational technologies. The ROC Story Cloze Task (SCT), introduced by Mostow and colleagues [1], serves as a popular benchmark for evaluating the performance of systems in predicting the logical ending to a short story from two candidate options. In this task, a model must determine which of the two provided endings best fits the preceding context, considering not only the grammatical and lexical consistency but also the narrative coherence and semantic plausibility. The challenge of story ending prediction lies in understanding the sequence of events, the underlying relationships between entities, and the causal structure that leads up to the conclusion. Traditional approaches focused on rule-based systems or extracted manually engineered features to model story structure and meaning. However, these methods often lack the flexibility and generalization needed for capturing the nuanced semantics and narrative complexity of human language. Recently, data-driven neural network-based models have been introduced to tackle this problem by learning representations directly from the data. In this paper, we propose a novel neural network architecture designed to improve the accuracy of story ending prediction. Our model, termed Multi-Attention based Neural Network (MANN), introduces multiple attention mechanisms at various levels of processing to capture both local and global semantic dependencies within the story. The utilization of attention mechanisms allows the model to dynamically allocate focus to the most relevant parts of the story, which is critical for maintaining coherence in narrative understanding. Additionally, inspired by the success of Highway Networks [2] in deep neural architectures, we incorporate Highway Units into our model to facilitate better gradient flow and more effective learning across deeper network layers. A key contribution of this work is the integration of   external knowledge sources   into our MANN model. We hypothesize that supplementing the model with external semantic resources—such as commonsense knowledge graphs, lexical databases (e.g., WordNet), and task-specific entity databases—can significantly improve the model's understanding of events, roles, and their interactions within the narrative. This external knowledge is embedded into our neural model using a carefully designed fusion mechanism that dynamically weighs the contributions of both the internal learned representations and the external knowledge sources.

Unsupervised Relation Extraction (URE) is an important problem in natural language processing, particularly relevant in domains where annotated corpora are limited or non-existent. Its objective is to identify relations between entities in text without pre-defined semantic types, relying instead on general language processing techniques and statistical patterns. Traditional URE systems typically use a two-step approach: first, they construct a vector space model (VSM) over entity pairs and linguistic patterns, and second, they apply clustering algorithms to group similar entity pairs under common semantic relations. While these systems have demonstrated some success, they often struggle with low clustering accuracy due to the inherent noise in pattern representations and the under-specification of features to capture complex semantic relationships. In this paper, we address the limitations of URE by introducing an informed feature generation method based on syntactic dependency trees. Dependency-based features provide a more precise and linguistically meaningful representation of entity relations and the syntactic structure of the text, enhancing the clusterability of entity pairs. We show that using these features significantly improves the quality of relation discovery, as measured by the F-score compared to standard bag-of-words and surface pattern-based features. Our experiments confirm that this syntactic enrichment leads to more coherent and semantically distinct clusters, enabling the URE framework to uncover meaningful and previously unknown relations with greater precision. Beyond relation discovery, we extend the traditional URE pipeline by introducing a method for generating discriminative extraction patterns associated with each identified relation. These patterns are weighted using the theory of Discriminative Category Matching (DCM), a generative probabilistic framework that evaluates the strength and reliability of a pattern in evoking a particular semantic relation. By assigning a confidence weight to each pattern, our model not only facilitates better pattern selection but also improves the robustness of downstream information extraction (IE) systems that rely on these patterns to generalize to unseen instances. A given pattern may be linked to one or more relations with varying degrees of confidence, enabling the system to adapt more flexibly to the semantics of the text. We evaluate our contributions on two benchmark relation extraction tasks against strong unsupervised and semi-supervised baselines. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in both relation discovery and accurate pattern induction. The URE system outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised methods in F1 scores, while the induced patterns show comparable performance to manually annotated rule-based systems in a downstream IE task.

Paraphrase detection is a central problem in natural language processing, with wide-ranging applications such as machine translation, information retrieval, and question answering. The task involves determining whether two sentences express the same meaning, regardless of their surface syntactic differences. Achieving robust and accurate paraphrase detection is challenging due to the vast variability in how meaning can be expressed in natural language, often requiring the system to look beyond surface-level lexical and syntactic cues. In recent years, deep learning approaches have set the state-of-the-art for paraphrase detection, leveraging large-scale data and carefully engineered features to model the semantic similarity between sentences. However, while these models succeed in capturing broad patterns, they often lack interpretability and struggle with out-of-distribution examples, especially when trained on datasets that are limited in scope or domain. As a result, there is a growing interest in hybrid approaches that combine the strengths of deep learning and hand-crafted semantic representations. One such semantic representation is the Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR). AMR is a graph-based representation that captures the core propositional semantics of a sentence while abstracting away from surface syntactic variation. This makes it particularly attractive for semantic equivalence tasks like paraphrase detection, as it aims to denote meaning in a canonical form independent of linguistic surface form. In this paper, we investigate the effectiveness of using AMR for paraphrase detection, with a particular focus on the Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus (MRPC), a widely used benchmark for evaluating the paraphrase identification task. Our initial experiments using naïve AMR features reveal that simply comparing AMR graphs is insufficient for achieving strong performance in paraphrase detection. This suggests that while AMR captures semantic content, it lacks the additional context and latent relationships needed to fully capture the nuanced equivalence required for paraphrase comparison. To address this limitation, we propose a hybrid approach that combines AMR parsing with latent semantic analysis (LSA). Our method projects AMR-based semantic features into a low-dimensional latent space, allowing the model to capture both the structural similarity of meaning representations and the distributional similarity between paraphrases. This technique not only enhances the effectiveness of AMR as a source of semantic content but also bridges the gap between syntactic-level deep learning models and abstract semantic representations. We evaluate our approach in both the inductive and transductive settings of the MRPC dataset. Our best-performing model achieves 86.6% accuracy and 90.0% F1 score in the transductive setting, outperforming several prior deep learning baselines.

The ability to accurately assess and quantify semantic atypicality in language production is a critical component of both clinical and empirical investigations into developmental language disorders, particularly in neurodevelopmental conditions like autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Language produced by children with ASD is often characterized by anomalies in semantics, including the use of words or phrases that appear unusual or unexpected within a given context (Koehler et al., 2011). These "unexpected" words often deviate from typical semantic expectations and can reflect difficulties in pragmatic understanding, lexical access, or conceptual integration. Despite their diagnostic and functional significance, the quantitative evaluation of such semantic anomalies has received relatively limited attention in both computational linguistics and clinical language research. Traditional methods for analyzing disordered language, particularly in children, have relied heavily on manual coding by trained clinicians or experimenters. While these methods offer high inter-rater reliability and rich interpretability, they are also labor-intensive, subjective to an extent, and often lack the capacity for large-scale analysis of language production across a continuous range of semantic variability. Recent advances in distributional semantics offer a promising, scalable, and objective alternative. Distributional semantic models (DSMs), grounded in the distributional hypothesis, represent words as dense vectors in a high-dimensional space, where semantic similarity is approximated by cosine distance or other geometric measures (Harris, 1954; Mikolov et al., 2013). In this paper, we explore the application of DSMs to the domain of disordered language, with a focus on distinguishing language patterns in children with autism from typically developing (TD) peers. Our goal is to quantify the prominence of "unexpected" language use through an automated paradigm that does not require pre-defined rules or lexicons of atypical items. We employ DSMs trained on large, general-purpose corpora to evaluate the extent to which certain lexical choices deviate from expected semantic contexts in narrative retellings. These retellings, elicited as a standardized language task in clinical and experimental settings, provide a naturalistic source of language data that captures both syntactic and semantic variation. We hypothesize that DSMs can effectively model typical semantic expectations, thereby enabling the reliable identification of lexically atypical words that are more frequently used by children with ASD. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that the proportion of such "unexpected" words serves as a diagnostically valuable feature that can reliably differentiate between the language of children with ASD and that of TD children. Notably, our method is language-agnostic in principle and can, in the future, be extended to other diagnostic populations or multilingual contexts.

The comparative analysis of two sentences is a foundational task in natural language processing (NLP), relevant to a wide range of real-world applications, including question answering, paraphrasing, machine translation, and textual entailment. The goal is to assess the relationship between two pieces of text, such as their semantic similarity, logical entailment, or relevance. Traditional approaches to sentence comparison often focus on either the word level—where relationships are modeled as pointwise interactions between individual words—or the sentence level—where features from one or both sentences are aggregated and matched as global vectors or embeddings. While these methods are effective in many scenarios, they often discard or underutilize the compositional and hierarchical structure of language, which is critical for capturing deeper syntactic and semantic relationships. A promising direction is to model the alignment between sentences at a structural level. For instance, syntactic or semantic parses provide explicit structural relationships, which can be leveraged for matching. However, in most prior work, such structures are incorporated as non-differentiable features derived from external parsers (e.g., constituency, dependency, or semantic role labels). This limits the model's ability to learn from the matching objective directly and opens the door to error propagation, as noisy or incorrect parse structures can mislead the learning process. Moreover, the real-world utility of these external features is constrained by the availability and accuracy of task-specific linguistic annotations. In this paper, we address these limitations by introducing   Structured Alignment Networks (SANs)  , a new model for matching sentences by simultaneously discovering their latent syntactic or semantic tree structures using a fully differentiable attention mechanism. Our key insight is to learn the sentence structures from unannotated data by designing a joint architecture where the alignment process is tied to the discovery of hierarchical relationships within and between the input sentences. Specifically, we use a structured attention mechanism that iteratively matches candidate spans—substrings of different lengths—from the first sentence to overlapping spans in the second sentence. This comparison is informed by the contextual embeddings of these spans and the evolutionary structure of previously matched pairs. The model inherently generates latent tree structures for both sentences during the alignment process without relying on any external parser. What distinguishes our model is its ability to jointly learn the latent structures and their inter-sentence alignment from a single matching objective. By end-to-end training with respect to the task of interest (e.g., entailment or relevance), the model can optimize the structures in a way that best supports the matching task, rather than depending on potentially suboptimal, out-of-distribution annotations.

Terminology acquisition is a crucial task in various fields of natural language processing, especially in domains where precise and specialized vocabulary is essential—such as medicine, law, or engineering. In particular, the extraction of multi-word terms from comparable corpora is a challenging but promising area of research, as it allows for the identification of domain-specific terminology without the need for parallel data. Comparable corpora are collections of texts that are not translations of each other but correspond in topic, genre, and style, typically across different languages. While these corpora are abundant, identifying equivalent terms across them—especially in the absence of explicit sentence alignments—requires robust and well-designed methods. One of the dominant approaches for terminology acquisition from comparable corpora is the compositional method, which leverages word alignment and the assumption that corresponding terms in each language share the same structure. However, traditional compositional approaches often suffer from limitations, especially when dealing with multi-word terms. These methods typically focus on aligning similar structures and fail to account for the nuanced contextual relationships that are critical in distinguishing between competing lexical candidates and their equivalents in another language. This shortcoming can lead to low precision, particularly in complex domains such as medicine, where terminology is both technical and context-sensitive. In this paper, we introduce the Compositional Method with Context-Based Projection (CMCBP), a revised and enhanced version of the compositional method designed to improve the alignment of equivalent terms from bilingual comparable corpora. The key contribution of CMCBP lies in its integration of contextual cues at both the lexical and phraseological levels. By incorporating principles from bilingual context projection, the proposed method enriches the matching criteria to account for the surrounding semantic environment of a term, thereby increasing the accuracy of identifying translationally equivalent multi-word expressions. Specifically, the CMCBP approach builds upon a two-stage process: (1) monolingual term extraction from each corpus, and (2) bilingual alignment using context-based projections to identify equivalent terms across languages. This context-based projection step incorporates semantic similarity metrics over local and global contexts, improving the robustness of the alignment and reducing the ambiguity inherent in traditional phrase-based matching. We demonstrate the efficacy of CMCBP in the medical domain, where accurate terminology mapping is of paramount importance. Through rigorous experimentation on two language pairs, we show that CMCBP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art compositional methods in both precision and recall, confirming its value as a promising direction for terminology acquisition from comparable corpora.

Punctuation plays a critical role in the syntactic and semantic structure of written language, providing cues about sentence boundaries, grammatical structure, and emphasis. However, in the output of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems, punctuation is typically omitted, resulting in long, unbroken sequences of words that lack the contextual clues necessary for downstream natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as parsing, summarization, and machine translation. The absence of punctuation can lead to ambiguity in sentence structure and meaning, making it difficult to apply modeling techniques that rely on grammatical or prosodic markers. To address this challenge, this paper presents a novel approach to punctuation prediction that leverages the power of transition-based parsing to simultaneously process syntactic features and infer appropriate punctuation marks in transcribed speech texts. Traditional approaches to punctuation prediction rely on rule-based heuristics or statistical models, such as maximum entropy or hidden Markov models, which often treat punctuation as an isolated task, considering only local contextual features. However, these models tend to ignore the rich syntactic context in which punctuation is embedded, which is particularly important for accurately predicting complex punctuation sequences in spoken language. In contrast, our method integrates syntactic information into a transition-based parsing framework, where each step in the parsing process is augmented with feature-based decisions for punctuation placement. This allows for a more linguistically informed and globally consistent model of punctuation inference. A key innovation of our approach is the joint modeling of parsing and punctuation prediction, where the system processes words in a left-to-right manner and uses a dynamic programming strategy to maintain a global view of the sentence. Our transition-based parser leverages a diverse set of syntactic features, including part-of-speech tags, phrase structure markers, and contextual dependencies, to guide the prediction of punctuation marks such as periods, commas, and question marks. Importantly, our formulation enables the model to capture long-range dependencies with linear time complexity, a crucial property for maintaining efficiency when processing large speech corpora. To assess the effectiveness of our method, we conducted extensive experiments on the benchmark datasets IWSLT and TDT4, which contain transcribed speech data with ground-truth punctuation annotations. The results demonstrate that our transition-based approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of punctuation prediction accuracy, outperforming previous models that do not incorporate syntactic parsing. Furthermore, our model's ability to jointly reason about syntactic structure and punctuation context provides insight into the linguistic motivations for punctuation use in speech, opening new avenues for improving the interpretability of NLP systems.

The task of translating text into sign language, particularly in the context of machine translation, presents a number of unique challenges, especially when it comes to the accurate representation of linguistic elements such as connectives. Connectives, such as  ma  ("but"),  e  ("and"), and  perché  ("because") in Italian, serve a pivotal role in structuring discourse and signaling the relationships between clauses and ideas. In spoken languages, these words often carry subtle logical, pragmatic, and semantic roles that must be preserved in translation. However, sign languages like LIS (Italian Sign Language) exhibit a fundamentally different morphosyntactic and grammatical structure from written/spoken languages, including expressivity made possible through spatial, gestural, and iconic features. These features are well-known to influence how linguistic elements, including function words and discourse markers, are expressed. LIS, as a natural language used by the Italian Deaf community, differs in structure and expressivity from Italian. This divergence is particularly evident when translating grammatical elements such as connectives, which, in the absence of direct equivalents, often require either the use of specific signs, lexical substitution, or even syntactic restructuring, and sometimes may be omitted entirely if the logical relationship is already encoded in the spatial or grammatical structure of LIS. As a result, accurate and faithful translation of such elements from Italian into LIS is a complex task that requires a deep understanding of both languages' structures and the communicative role of connectives in discourse. This paper addresses the underexplored task of translating Italian connectives into LIS, focusing on how different connectives are represented in the target language. Due to the limited availability of annotated corpora that include both Italian sentences and their LIS translations, we propose a method based on the alignment of syntactic trees between Italian and LIS. This approach enables us to map verbal expressions to LIS constructions systematically, even when direct one-to-one equivalences do not exist. Furthermore, by clustering the translated connectives based on their mapping patterns, we uncover the varied strategies employed in LIS for expressing logical relations, such as the use of specific manual signs, spatial indicators, or silent omission. Our findings reveal that a single Italian connective can be rendered in LIS in multiple ways, depending on the discourse context and the surrounding signs. For example, the conjunctive  e  may be represented by a specific sign like  E  (the go-to equivalent), but it may also be expressed through spatial adjacency or even silently left out, especially when the coordination is evident from the visual syntax of the sentence.

Textual entailment is a central problem in natural language understanding, involving the determination of whether a given hypothesis can be logically inferred from a premise text. Cross-lingual textual entailment (CLTE) extends this problem to cases where the premise and hypothesis are presented in different languages, introducing additional challenges such as language-specific syntax, polysemy, and the need for robust translation mechanisms. These challenges are often exacerbated by the lack of annotated cross-lingual entailment datasets, which limits the scalability and generalizability of modeling approaches. In recent years, machine learning and deep learning models have demonstrated impressive performance on monolingual entailment tasks (e.g., GLUE, SuperGLUE benchmarks), but cross-lingual scenarios remain significantly less explored due to both data scarcity and the complexity of accurately modeling cross-lingual semantic equivalence. This paper investigates how bilingual parallel corpora, a widely available and underutilized resource in entailment modeling, can be leveraged to improve CLTE systems. We argue that such corpora inherently encode rich lexical and syntactic relationships across languages, particularly when aligned at the sentence or phrase level. By extracting phrase tables directly from parallel data, we can represent multilingual semantic patterns without relying on explicit translation models or strong linguistic annotations. Contrary to the common assumption that parallel corpora are primarily useful for machine translation or bilingual lexicon induction, we propose that they can serve as a rich source of lexical and contextual information for reasoning and inference tasks across languages. Central to our approach is the use of a phrasal matching method, designed to identify lexical and co-occurrence patterns in parallel corpora. This not only facilitates a comparison of semantic content across premise and hypothesis in different languages but also ensures a system that is modular, interpretable, and generalizable across language pairs. Notably, our system is engineered to evaluate the contribution of lexical knowledge  in isolation , without relying on or interfering with other inference mechanisms such as syntactic dependency matching or semantic role labeling. This allows for a clearer understanding of the role that bilingual phrase tables can play in cross-lingual reasoning, and opens the door for integrating such knowledge into more complex, hybrid models. Our experiments focus on an English-Spanish cross-lingual entailment corpus derived from the RTE3 dataset, a well-known benchmark in textual entailment. By applying our phrasal matching method and incorporating bilingual knowledge from the European Parliament's parallel corpora, we demonstrate significant improvements over monolingual baseline systems and achieve an overall accuracy that outperforms previously reported results on similar tasks.

The automated extraction of bilingual data from the Web is crucial for many natural language processing applications such as machine translation, cross-language information retrieval, and terminology extraction. Despite significant progress in this area, existing methods often struggle with the heterogeneity and scale of real-world web pages, which contain a mixture of multilingual content, advertisements, footers, and nested structures that obscure coherent bilingual passages. Traditional approaches either rely on heuristics specific to particular web domains or use expensive transcription-based methods to identify parallel content. In contrast, we propose a novel,   adaptive pattern-based method   for mining bilingual pairs from the Web that learns from the data itself. Our approach is motivated by the observation that bilingual content often co-occurs in web pages and is frequently associated with web structures and layout that follow repeated, albeit not identical, patterns. These patterns can be captured by analyzing the relationships between text segments in the page and using translation pairs identified as local anchors or "seeds" to generalize better. This, in turn, allows us to extract bilingual data dynamically in a way that adapts to different websites and content types. The method follows a four-step pipeline. First, during preprocessing, the raw HTML of a web page is parsed into a   Document Object Model (DOM)   tree. Each node of the tree is then segmented into smaller textual units, or   snippets  , which are used as the building blocks for downstream processing. Second,   seed mining   leverages a word-based alignment model that considers both   translation and transliteration cues   to identify the initial bilingual pairs. These seeds are crucial because they act as starting points for the pattern-learning phase. Third,   pattern learning   generates rules that generalize the linguistic and layout-based collocations observed in the extracted seeds. Unlike rigid syntactic rules, our patterns are probabilistic and context-sensitive, derived from DOM contexts and positional dependencies. Finally, in the   pattern-based mining   stage, the learned patterns are applied to the entire DOM tree to extract a comprehensive set of bilingual sentence and term pairs from the web page. We evaluate our method on a large collection of Chinese web pages and show that it is highly effective at extracting   bilingual data at scale  . Specifically, we are able to extract over 7.5 million bilingual sentence pairs and over 5 million bilingual term pairs with   an accuracy of over 80%  , as measured by manual sampling and filtering experiments.

Chinese event extraction remains a challenging task due to the inherent difficulties of the Chinese language, such as the lack of explicit word boundaries, syntactic flexibility, and the often ambiguous co-reference relations that complicate event modeling. More importantly, existing systems are severely hampered by two major issues in the annotation of event corpora. First, the quality of Chinese event annotations is generally low, with a high proportion of noisy or inconsistent examples attributable to the labor-intensive and error-prone nature of manual annotation in this under-resourced language. Second, due to the large number of candidate triggers—words or phrases that may indicate an event—the ratio of pseudo trigger mentions (non-event words incorrectly annotated as triggers) to true triggers is high, leading to the frequent misclassification of non-event expressions and poor model generalization. These issues pose significant obstacles to the development of accurate and robust Chinese event extraction systems, especially when relying on traditional pipeline or single-task modeling approaches that treat trigger identification and event type determination as separate, sequential tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel joint modeling approach that simultaneously identifies trigger words and determines the corresponding event types. By integrating the two stages into a shared architecture, the model can better exploit the interdependence between trigger characteristics and event semantics, leading to improved end-to-end performance. For instance, while a word like “发生” ( fāshēng , “happen”) can be a strong indicator of an event, its relevance may vary depending on the event type (e.g., Conflict, Disasters, Business Transactions), and the event type can also constrain the possible set of valid triggers. The proposed joint model also introduces trigger filtering schemas to reduce the number of pseudo trigger mentions. These schemas leverage the internal consistency of trigger and event type labels through voting mechanisms and contextual constraints to effectively eliminate noisy candidates before downstream processing. Experimental results on the widely used ACE 2005 Chinese corpus demonstrate that our joint model and filtering mechanisms significantly outperform strong baselines and handle the scarcity and noise in annotated data more effectively. This approach not only advances the state of the art in Chinese event extraction but also provides a blueprint for improving event modeling in other under-resourced languages, where similar issues of corpus quality and input noise are prevalent. The ability to jointly model triggers and their corresponding events, while minimizing the impact of pseudo triggers, represents a critical step forward in delivering more accurate and reliable machine reading systems for real-world event-centric information processing tasks.

Recent advancements in machine translation (MT) have emphasized the effectiveness of combining outputs from multiple MT systems to enhance translation accuracy and fluency. Among various system combination techniques, confusion network (CN) decoding has emerged as a state-of-the-art method due to its ability to process multiple system outputs and search for the optimal translation path through a lattice structure that captures all possible word sequences from the input systems. Despite its success, one of the major challenges in efficiently constructing a confusion network lies in the hypothesis alignment process—specifically, aligning words between the   backbone hypothesis   (the primary or reference MT output) and the   other hypotheses   generated by different MT systems. This alignment is complicated by the fact that neighboring MT systems often differ in word order and phrase structures, particularly across language pairs with morphological richness or syntactic divergence. Hypothesis alignment typically relies on word alignment tools, which aim to establish correspondences between the words of the source and target sentences—or, in the context of MT system combination, between the words of two or more MT outputs. Various word alignment methods have been proposed, including GIZA++ (based on IBM models), TER (Translation Error Rate) alignments, CLA (Constrained Lexical Alignment), and IHMM (Iterative Hidden Markov Model). While these methods vary in their alignment strategies and assumptions, their integration into the hypothesis alignment step is crucial for ensuring that the confusion network fairly represents the alignment-based intersections and differences among the MT outputs. In this paper, we conduct a   comparative study   of the four word alignment methods—GIZA++, TER, CLA, and IHMM—when applied to the hypothesis alignment task in the context of confusion network-based MT system combination. We then propose an   improvement strategy   that utilizes   intersection word alignment  , which combines both   direct   (backbone to hypothesis) and   inverse   (hypothesis to backbone) alignments to enhance the robustness and precision of the alignment process. This intersection-based approach addresses the issues of one-sided bias that often arise when only a single alignment direction is used. To evaluate the effectiveness of our alignment strategy, we conduct experiments on both   Chinese-to-English spoken language   and   Chinese-to-English written language   translation tasks. Our results demonstrate that the proposed intersection alignment method leads to   consistent improvements   in system combination performance across all four word alignment methods considered. Moreover, we analyze the impact of each alignment component and highlight the practical benefits of incorporating bidirectional alignment information into the hypothesis alignment phase.

Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has achieved remarkable success through the use of large-scale bilingual corpora. However, the development and curation of such datasets often require significant human effort, particularly in resource-constrained or low-resource language pairs where parallel texts are scarce or non-existent. While parallel corpora for well-resourced languages (such as English, German, French, and Spanish) are increasingly available, the same is not true for many languages represented in ambitious transcription efforts, such as the widely used EuroParl corpus, which contains records of European Parliament session documents. Traditionally, the process of bootstrapping MT systems for a new language has relied on manual annotation, which is both time-consuming and prone to error, especially at scale. This paper investigates the use of  active learning  as a viable and efficient alternative to manual annotation for extending multilingual SMT systems. Active learning, a well-established technique in the machine learning community, is particularly relevant when labeled data is sparse or expensive to obtain. The core idea behind active learning is to iteratively select the most informative sentences for annotation, which are expected to provide the most benefit to the ML model in improving its performance with each iteration. This is in contrast to the typical passive learning setup, where data is annotated in a random or uniform manner. In the context of SMT, active learning is a natural fit because paraphrases, syntactic variation, and semantic verbosity are core properties of translation, making every new annotation potentially informative. In this work, we extend the active learning paradigm to the setting of  multilingual SMT , where the goal is not to build a translation system for a single language pair, but to establish a new  target  language as part of a previously existing multilingual collection of parallel texts. That is, we are given a set of $n$ source languages already aligned to a language $T$, and we aim to extend this collection by adding a new source language $L_{n+1}$, translated into $T$, using a limited budget of annotated sentences. To achieve high-quality translation, the active learning process must strike a balance between sampling sentences that are  lexically diverse , accurate, and syntactically rich while being representative of the target domain. The challenge is further compounded by the fact that a new translation system must operate in harmony with the existing multilingual set, where source-to-target alignments may exhibit context-dependent syntactic or semantic shifts.

Natural language understanding systems often employ a pipeline architecture, in which the output of one component is used as input for the next. A classic example of this is the flow from syntactic parsing to semantic role labeling (SRL), where a constituent or dependency parser generates a syntactic structure, and a semantic role labeler (SRL system) uses that structure to identify predicates and label the roles of their arguments within the sentence. This unidirectional data flow has been effective in many applications, but it also has a key limitation: errors introduced at earlier stages are not corrected as the system proceeds. Parser errors propagate into the SRL, and the decision made by the SRL is not fed back into the system to improve earlier stages. Recent advances in joint modeling and integration have shown that allowing components to jointly influence one another can lead to significant improvements in overall system accuracy. In this paper, we explore the potential of   bidirectional interaction   between a syntactic parser and an SRL system. Specifically, we investigate how semantic predictions can improve the quality of syntactic parses, and how corrected parses, in turn, improve final SRL performance. One challenge in directly integrating semantic labelers into the parsing process is the computational cost—SRL typically requires a well-formed parse to extract meaningful features. For instance, many semantic features in current SRL systems are based on phrase-structure or dependency relations derived from the parser’s output, making it difficult to perform semantic reasoning during parsing itself. Instead, we propose a system that   uses semantic role predictions to re-score and re-order a list of n-best parses  . Our key insight is that a semantic role labeler can serve as a discriminative model over possible parse structures: parses that are inconsistent with the semantic roles being annotated are less probable and should be discarded. This is achieved in two stages. First, a   baseline parser generates a set of high-plausibility parses  , which are then passed to a semantic role scor- ing model. The scoring model combines both syntactic and semantic features to distinguish high-quality parses from those likely to cause errors in downstream roles. The scored parses are then re-ranked, with higher ranks assigned to parses that are more consistent with strong semantic role predictions. Second, we explore a more direct form of integration by   modifying a semantic role labeler to operate at parse-time  , even though its feature set is restricted by the information available in the parser's intermediate representation (e.g., the packed chart or partial parse trees).

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled impressive capabilities in high-level language generation tasks such as machine translation, text summarization, and image captioning. As these systems become increasingly complex, a reliable and nuanced evaluation methodology becomes essential for tracking progress and understanding model behavior. Traditionally, automatic evaluation metrics like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), ROUGE (Lin, 2004), and METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005) have been used as proxies for human judgment. While these metrics broadly correlate with human assessment, they often fall short in capturing the fine-grained aspects of language quality—such as fluency, coherence, factual accuracy, or syntactic structure that may be undesirable or preferred in different contexts. Moreover, the subjective and variable nature of human judgment introduces inconsistency into the evaluation process: studies (Asmus et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2017) have frequently reported low inter- and intra-annotator agreement when evaluating generations, even among experts. This raises critical questions: To what extent do current metrics align with the aspects of language quality we want to measure? And, more importantly, do they fail in consistent and predictable ways that we can characterize and improve upon? To address these concerns, we propose MUTT (Metric Unit TesTing), a framework for evaluating the robustness and sensitivity of language generation metrics to systematic transformations of text. MUTT treats metric evaluation as a form of unit testing, where we apply controlled, atomic changes to generated text—what we refer to as "corruptions"—and examine whether the resulting changes in metric scores align with human intuitions and linguistic expectations. For example, transforming a sentence from active to passive voice, omitting function words, or syntactically reordering constituents while preserving semantic content can be used to assess whether a metric captures important linguistic properties or treats syntactically divergent but semantically equivalent sentences equitably. MUTT offers a structured alternative to traditional human-annotated evaluation by isolating minimal examples where any metric's preferences or biases can be clearly observed. The unit testing perspective allows us to pinpoint specific failure modes of a metric, which is often challenging using aggregate correlation statistics. More importantly, such analysis can reveal systematic weaknesses—such as a lack of syntactic sensitivity, over-penalization of paraphrase, or insufficient sensitivity to sentence-level fluency features—thereby guiding the design of improved evaluation methods. In this paper, we conduct a case study applying MUTT to three widely used automatic evaluation metrics: BLEU, ROUGE, and METEOR, alongside a more modern model-based score from BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2020).

Information retrieval (IR) systems are fundamentally designed to bridge the gap between users and unstructured text data by identifying documents that best match a given query. Traditional IR techniques such as the vector space model and probabilistic retrieval models focus on matching documents and queries at the level of individual terms, typically using co-occurrence statistics and term frequencies. While these methods are effective, they often fail to account for   semantic relationships among terms  , which are crucial for a deeper understanding of document content. For example, a query containing the term "car" may arguably be relevant to documents that include terms like "automobile" or "vehicle," yet such relationships are often not captured by standard methods without explicit query expansion. Additionally, term frequency-based approaches may not adequately reflect the   importance of a term within a document   (e.g., discounting common terms like "the" via an inverse document frequency mechanism), and they often lack the ability to model complex document structure at a conceptual level. In this paper, we present a   probabilistic generative modeling approach   to IR using   Hierarchical Dirichlet Trees (HDTs)  . The model is built upon a principled framework that imposes a tree structure over the vocabulary space, allowing the system to capture both local and global relationships among terms. The tree inherently enables inferences about relatedness, by assigning higher probability to documents that contain terms located near each other in the hierarchy. This leads to an implicit form of   query expansion  —whereby the system retrieves documents containing terms semantically similar to those in the query—without requiring explicit expansion by the user or the system. Furthermore, the model naturally exhibits a behavior analogous to   inverse document frequency (IDF)   by assigning lower weights to terms that are common across many documents, but which may not be particularly informative in retrieving relevant content. The hierarchical Dirichlet tree represents the underlying generative process of document construction as follows: at the top level, each document is modeled as a distribution over topics, and each topic, in turn, is associated with a subset of the tree (possibly spanning multiple branches). Document generation then proceeds by sampling terms from topics, with the frequency of each term depending on its position in the tree and its apparent informativeness as captured by the Dirichlet distribution over tree nodes. This hierarchical structure provides a compact yet expressive way of encoding both the   semantic proximity of terms   and the   importance of specific terms within a document or corpus  .

Recent advancements in machine translation have significantly benefited from effective word segmentation strategies, particularly when dealing with languages that lack clear word boundaries, such as Chinese or Arabic. Word segmentation is a critical preprocessing step for both source and target sentences, as inaccurate segmentation can lead to poor translation quality and alignment errors. Traditional approaches to word segmentation can be broadly categorized into two types: rule-based and statistical models. Rule-based methods rely on predefined linguistic knowledge and heuristics, while statistical models exploit large corpora to learn segmentation patterns automatically. However, these approaches are often either language-specific or require annotated training data, which is difficult and expensive to obtain in many low-resource scenarios. Moreover, these methods typically perform monolingual segmentation in isolation, without considering the influence of the target language during the segmentation process. In this work, we present a nonparametric unsupervised model for word segmentation in the source language, designed specifically for the purpose of machine translation. Our model integrates monolingual segmentation techniques with bilingual word alignment, allowing the segmentation process in the source language to be informed by the relationships between words in the source and target languages. Specifically, the model jointly infers the segmentation of the source sentence and the corresponding word alignments to the target sentence. Unlike traditional two-step approaches where segmentation is performed independently and only later used for translation, our method couples these processes during inference. The monolingual segmentation model is guided by the information extracted from the alignment model, and vice versa, enabling a more coherent and context-aware segmentation of source sentences. This integration allows for dynamic and adaptive splits that align more meaningfully with the target sentence structure. The model does not rely on fixed linguistic rules or a predefined dictionary, making it a flexible and language-agnostic approach. It operates in a nonparametric Bayesian framework, allowing the number of segments or word units in the source sentence to grow as needed based on the data, which is particularly advantageous for document-length or low-resource settings. The model is trained and evaluated using a fully unsupervised workflow, requiring no manual segmentation for either the source or target sentences. Our experimental evaluations are conducted on two challenging language pairs: Arabic-English and Chinese-English. The results demonstrate that our approach achieves significant improvements in translation performance compared to strong baseline models that employ independent word segmentation strategies. These gains underscore the value of leveraging the interaction between the source-side segmentation process and the target-side alignment process.

The task of identifying online review pages is a foundational problem in web mining and information retrieval. Review pages are valuable sources of real-time user sentiment, product feedback, and consumer behavior insights across various domains such as e-commerce, media, and services. Traditionally, supervised approaches to this problem require extensive manually labeled datasets, where each web page is annotated as a review or non-review based on linguistic, structural, and contextual cues. However, the labor-intensive nature of such labeling hinders the scalability and adaptability of these methods, especially when applied across large, heterogeneous domains or under resource-constrained settings. Hence, the question arises: can we identify review pages at scale without the prior investment of human-labeled training data? In this paper, we propose an unsupervised method that addresses the challenge of identifying online review pages without relying on any human-annotated labels. Our approach integrates two key ideas: (1) the construction of a classifier using a large number of noisy examples, and (2) the leveraging of the structural context of a website to refine and enhance classification performance. The first component, the building of a classifier from noisy examples, is realized through the use of automatically mined text patterns—such as page titles, anchor texts, and metadata—that are frequently associated with review pages. These patterns are derived from a large corpus of webpage data, circumventing the need for labeled training sets. While the resulting examples are often noisy, with significant variation in structure and content, we employ a robust classification algorithm capable of handling such uncertainty. The second component addresses one of the critical limitations of feature-based classification in this domain: the ambiguity of individual cues. To overcome this, we incorporate topological and navigational information from the website, such as the interlinking structure, section placement, and proximity to other known or likely review pages. This structural enhancement significantly boosts the classifier's ability to distinguish review pages from pages with similar lexical or stylistic features but different underlying purposes. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves performance that is competitive, and in many cases superior, to well-known supervised baselines. For instance, on benchmark evaluation sets used previously in the literature, our system achieves an accurate identification rate that rivals those of models trained on human-labeled data. Furthermore, we observe that integrating the structural website features not only improves accuracy but also leads to more consistent and robust predictions, even in the face of noisy or contextually complex features.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled us to analyze and understand textual data from a wide range of real-world sources, including conversational dialogues from social media and customer service interactions. These dialogues often exhibit complex and hierarchical structures that are not only influenced by the content of individual utterances but also by temporal dependencies and shared topics across the conversation. Despite the importance of capturing such structures for dialogue understanding tasks such as intent recognition, sentiment analysis, and conversation summarization, traditional models often focus solely on sentence modeling or single-turn classification, which limits their ability to capture the full dynamics of dialogue. In particular, existing approaches typically rely on either probabilistic graphical models or neural sequence models (e.g., LSTMs and Transformers), which can struggle to uncover latent semantic hierarchies, such as recurring topics and global themes, that are critical for modeling the evolution of dialogues over time. To address these limitations, we present the hidden softmax sequence model (HSSM), a novel unsupervised learning approach inspired by the Boltzmann machine framework, designed specifically for dialogue structure analysis. The HSSM model introduces three distinct types of hidden units to learn and represent the underlying structures of dialogues: 1.   Latent states of utterances   represented by   softmax units  , which assign a distribution over possible hidden states for each dialogue turn, capturing the evolving context of the conversation. 2.   Latent topics per dialogue   represented by   binary topic units  , enabling the model to identify conversation-specific topics arising from the content and participant interactions. 3.   A single global topic unit  , which represents a shared theme or intent that spans the entire dialogue corpus, thereby capturing high-level discourse patterns and contextual consistency across dialogues. In addition to these hierarchical representations, the HSSM introduces extra connections between   adjacent softmax units  , modeling dependencies between latent states of consecutive utterances. This allows the model to not only uncover local coherence but also global coherence across the full conversation sequence. The model is trained in an unsupervised manner by maximizing the log-likelihood of the observed utterances, allowing it to infer both the latent states and topics without the need for explicit labels. We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed model using two diverse real-world dialogue corpora: 1.   Twitter-Post  , a collection of multi-turn conversations extracted from Twitter where users discuss various topics in the context of social media interactions. 2.   AirTicketBooking  , a dataset of simulated dialogues in the domain of air travel booking, where user-system interactions follow a predefined conversation structure.

The task of predicting linguistic structure—such as syntactic dependencies or named entities—has long benefited from the integration of features derived from word clusters, which are extracted from large unlabeled corpora and encode rich semantic and syntactic information about words. These clusters help capture the distributional properties of words and mitigate the data sparsity problem common in tasks involving rare or out-of-vocabulary terms. However, much of the previous work on using word clusters for improving linguistic prediction has focused heavily on English, leaving a significant gap in understanding how these techniques can be generalized to other languages. In this paper, we present a comprehensive study that explores the use of word clusters not only across language families but also as a means to improve cross-lingual transfer of linguistic structure prediction models. Our work addresses the challenge of transferring linguistic knowledge from a high-resource language, such as English, to low-resource target languages. We take two key approaches. First, we investigate whether word clusters trained independently on monolingual corpora—spanning languages from diverse language families—can be used to improve the performance of structure prediction models, such as dependency parsers and named-entity recognizers, in those languages. Our results confirm that, indeed, word cluster features contribute significantly across these languages, even when the clusters are not shared across language pairs. Second, we introduce a novel method for inducing cross-lingual word clusters that directly bridge the lexical spaces of source and target languages, without requiring explicit word alignments or parallel data. These clusters are derived from aligned pseudo-parallel corpora generated through the use of a word translation model, which allows for distributional similarity to be preserved across languages. By incorporating features derived from these cross-lingual clusters into structure prediction systems, we demonstrate a substantial improvement in cross-lingual transfer settings. To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we conduct experiments on two linguistic tasks: dependency parsing and named-entity recognition. In dependency parsing, we observe that delexicalized parsers trained on English and transferred to a target language show relative error reductions of up to 13% when augmented with cross-lingual cluster features. For named-entity recognition, where the task is particularly sensitive to lexical ambiguity, we achieve relative performance improvements of up to 26%. These results highlight the importance of explicitly modeling lexical relationships across languages and underscore the potential of cross-lingual word clusters for improving the accuracy of direct-transfer systems.

Dependency parsing is a core task in natural language processing (NLP), where the goal is to analyze the grammatical structure of a sentence by establishing relationships between words in the form of a labeled dependency tree. Traditionally, dependency parsing systems are trained on treebanks with rich syntactic annotations, such as universal dependencies (UD;De Marneffe et al., 2014). However, such annotated resources are often not available for many languages or domains. A more scalable and desirable alternative is  unsupervised dependency parsing , where the model learns to build dependency structures from raw text with only part-of-speech (POS) tag annotations (if any). This setting is particularly relevant for under-resourced languages where linguistic annotations are either absent or prohibitively expensive to create. Unsupervised methods must identify valid syntactic structures purely from the distributional patterns of words and their interactions, while relying on architectural choices or feature combinations to encode reasonable prior linguistic knowledge about the expected grammar. Classical unsupervised models often include handcrafted priors or inductive biases to regularize the learning space and guide the discovery of plausible grammatical rules (Klein and Manning, 2004; Petrov et al., 2006; Fossum et al., 2016). Among these, one important class of biases is based on the assumption that grammatical rules vary systematically depending on the POS tags of the head and dependent words. For example, nouns are often modified by adjectives and determiners, whereas verbs are commonly followed by objects or complements. Capturing such POS-specific correlations between grammar rules is essential for discovering a linguistically meaningful parse structure. Previous unsupervised approaches have incorporated these correlations either by manually encoding POS tag-based rules as part of the model's inductive bias or by using specialized prior distributions (e.g., parameter tying, Dirichlet priors) to enforce expected POS-related behavior during parameter estimation (Chandrasekar and Hall, 2013; Liang et al., 2009; Peng et al., 2016). However, these methods are confined by the need for prior engineering, restricting the flexibility of the model to discover potentially richer and more complex correlations from data. In this paper, we propose an unsupervised neural dependency parsing approach that leverages a  distributed representation of POS tags  to automatically model the correlations between POS-specific grammar rules.
