Traditional approaches to learning bilingual embeddings typically rely on parallel corpora or extensive dictionary resources to enforce alignment constraints between languages, often requiring complex models such as adversarial training (Ganin & Lempitsky, 2015), semantic projection methods (Mikolov et al., 2013), or iterative refinement procedures (Artetxe et al., 2018). While these methods have demonstrated success, they often demand substantial linguistic resources and are not easily adaptable to task-specific representations. In this paper, we propose a   simple and flexible method   for learning   task-specific bilingual word embeddings   using off-the-shelf embedding algorithms and   without requiring parallel data  . Our approach is based on a   wrapper method   that cleverly reuses existing context modeling techniques by introducing   mixed context-target pairs   derived from a   small dictionary of task-specific word equivalence classes  . By relaxing the assumption that full parallel corpora or dictionary mappings are available, we make bilingual embedding learning more accessible and adaptable to real-world tasks, especially in low-resource or cross-lingual settings. The core idea of our method rests on leveraging task-specific equivalence classes—these can, for example, be linguistic tags or semantic roles shared across languages (e.g., the translation of the English tag “NN” might correspond to the Russian tag “S1”). These classes are used to define a soft equivalence between words across language pairs. We construct a bilingual training set where   source and target words related through these equivalence classes are paired  , effectively forming "bilingual context pairs." Once this mixed bilingual corpus is created,   any standard word embedding algorithm  —from word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) to FastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017)—can be used to learn task-specific bilingual embeddings by treating the input as a regular monolingual corpus. Our method offers three major advantages. First,   it is agnostic to the word embedding model used  , enabling a plug-and-play integration with various state-of-the-art techniques. Second, it   eliminates the need for parallel data  , which is often costly or unattainable for low-resource language pairs. Third, the method is   task-adaptive  , allowing the embedding representations to be refined and specialized for diverse NLP applications simply by adjusting the definition of equivalence classes. To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we conduct experiments on two cross-lingual NLP tasks:   unsupervised cross-language part-of-speech (POS) tagging   and   semi-supervised cross-language super sense (SuS) tagging  .

Marginal inference is a fundamental task in a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) applications, as it enables the estimation of confidence measures, the computation of conditional likelihoods for training, and the implementation of posterior-based decoding strategies. In models with complex factor graphs and large output spaces, exact marginal inference is computationally expensive, if not intractable. This has led to the widespread use of approximate inference methods, such as belief propagation (BP) and its variants, which trade off some inference accuracy for efficiency. In recent years, relaxation techniques have emerged as a promising avenue to tackle the problem of finding the maximum a posteriori (MAP) assignment in NLP tasks. These methods iteratively relax the problem constraints, enabling the use of efficient optimization techniques on subproblems that approximate the original inference task. However, most existing work on relaxation has focused exclusively on the setting of MAP inference, leaving open the question of how to extend these techniques to the more complex and resource-intensive task of marginal inference. In this paper, we propose a generalization of relaxation techniques from MAP inference to marginal inference, which provides a scalable and flexible framework for approximating full marginal probabilities over output spaces with large, structured dependencies. Our method leverages the same decomposition principles used in relaxation to perform approximate computation of marginal distributions by limiting the scope of inference to a manageable subset of the full factor graph. This is particularly attractive for models where dependencies are local or can be represented in a hierarchical fashion, as the resulting subgraph often retains enough structural detail to yield high-quality marginal estimates. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in the context of dependency parsing, a canonical NLP task that benefits significantly from marginal inference. Specifically, we consider second-order dependency parsing models, which explicitly model the co-occurrence of labels between head-modifier pairs and their context, resulting in richer but more expensive inference. Our experiments show that by applying our relaxed marginal inference approach, we can reduce the size of the factor graph over which inference is performed while incurring no loss in predictive accuracy. Moreover, parsing speed increases by more than an order of magnitude compared to exact inference. This enables the use of complex marginal inference strategies in practice, where performance and scalability are critical. To further support the robustness of our approach, we also derive a theoretical bound on the error of the approximated marginals in comparison to the true marginals computed over the full factor graph.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have produced two highly influential paradigms for capturing latent semantics in text: topic modeling and word embedding. Topic modeling techniques, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) \cite{blei2003latent}, are powerful tools for uncovering high-level themes or topics within a corpus by analyzing word co-occurrence at the document or sentence level. These models typically focus on capturing global semantic patterns by aggregating statistics over large spans of text. In contrast, word embedding models, like Word2Vec \cite{mikolov2013distributed} and GloVe \cite{pennington2014glove}, operate at the level of small, local contexts by analyzing word co-occurrence within sliding windows. These approaches are particularly effective at modeling syntactic and semantic relationships between closely related words and generating dense, low-dimensional vector representations that capture fine-grained linguistic regularities. Despite their respective strengths, these two paradigms are traditionally treated as separate tasks, each designed to capture semantics at different granularities. This divide, however, limits the potential of each approach to benefit from the other's inductive biases and assumptions. While topic models are effective at discovering high-level semantic clusters, they often overlook the fine-grained relationships between words. Conversely, word embeddings struggle to infer broader semantic trends that span entire documents or large sections of text because they are constrained by their local context windows. To bridge this gap and unify the strengths of both paradigms, we propose a novel probabilistic model called \textit{Latent Topic Embedding} (LTE). LTE is designed to simultaneously learn global topic structures and local word representations in a cohesive and mutually reinforcing framework. By integrating topic modeling and word embedding into a single latent variable model, LTE captures the dual nature of semantic information: high-level thematic consistency and fine-grained lexical relationships. This integration is achieved by factorizing the joint distribution of topics and word embeddings within a shared latent space, allowing for coherent semantic representations at multiple levels of hierarchy. A key innovation of LTE is its use of an efficient Monte Carlo Expectation-Maximization (MC-EM) algorithm to estimate model parameters. This algorithm effectively handles the intractability of the joint distribution by approximating the Expectation step using variational inference and delivering stable convergence during the Maximization step. The MC-EM framework enables LTE to scale efficiently to large corpora while retaining high representational fidelity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LTE through extensive experiments on real-world NLP tasks, including semantic similarity, downstream document classification, and topic coherence evaluation.

Chinese word segmentation (CWS) is a foundational task in natural language processing, especially for Chinese and other languages where words are not separated by whitespace. Over the past decade, the performance of CWS systems has improved significantly due to the application of powerful supervised learning techniques. Most state-of-the-art methods rely on well-annotated corpora that provide high-quality examples of word boundaries. However, the effectiveness of these models depends heavily on the availability of a large and representative training dataset. In practice, this requirement poses a significant challenge when applying CWS systems to new domains, where annotated data are scarce or nonexistent. Supervised models, when faced with domain shifts or lack of domain-specific corpora, often fail to produce accurate results due to the poor generalization of their training. The problem of domain adaptation for CWS remains a major research challenge. While there has been progress in unsupervised and semi-supervised approaches, the accuracy of these methods is often far lower than their fully supervised counterparts, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios where performance matters. Additionally, the cost and time required to manually annotate large-scale corpora make it impractical to rely on domain-specific labeled data for each new application scenario. This limitation has spurred interest in exploring alternative methods for acquiring training data without human intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper proposes an innovative approach to   automatic corpus expansion   for CWS by leveraging the   redundancy and richness of web information  . The core idea is to exploit the web as a virtually limitless source of annotated sentences, where the segmentation of words, though not explicitly labeled, can be inferred using heuristic methods and linguistic patterns. When given a sentence that is difficult to segment due to domain-specific idioms or novel expressions, our method automatically queries the web for similar or syntactically related sentences. These mined sentences are often easier to segment, either due to their commonness or simpler grammatical structure. By transforming this redundant data into segmented examples and integrating it into the training corpus, the system effectively  bootstrap  itself to learn from domain-specific patterns. This approach does not rely on complex algorithmic enhancements or domain knowledge; instead, it shifts the focus toward automatically augmenting the training data. As such, it complements existing CWS research by offering a scalable and data-driven solution that can be rapidly deployed across domains. The method is particularly suitable for low-resource or rapidly evolving domains, such as social media, technical manuals, or niche professional jargons, where annotated datasets are either unavailable or insufficient.

Parsing disfluent speech—particularly speech that includes repairs such as repetitions, utterance-final reparanda, and self-corrections—remains a key challenge in natural language processing, especially in systems that aim to model or transcribe spoken language accurately. Unlike written text, speech is inherently dynamic and often includes corrective behaviors that can disrupt syntactic structure and complicate the assignment of meaningful representations. These disfluencies can significantly degrade the performance of standard syntactic parsers that are typically trained on or designed for fluent data. The conventional modeling approaches often treat reparanda and their repairs as isolated syntactic units, which can cause mismatches when processing the full disfluent utterance. However, a growing body of work suggests that linguistic repair is not just a surface-level phenomenon; it reflects deeper cognitive and grammatical processes that must be taken into account in syntactic modeling. This paper presents three novel syntactic models designed to improve the parsing of speech with repairs by encoding prior linguistic intuitions about when and how repairs are recognized and corrected. Our central hypothesis is that the reparandum—the part of an utterance that is subsequently corrected—should not be analyzed as full grammatical constituents during the initial utterance production but is rather identified as incorrect only in hindsight, after the repair has been made and the speaker's commitment has been signaled. These three models build on this idea and are structured to reflect different strategies for handling such delayed recognition while reducing the syntactic noise that disfluencies introduce. By minimizing the syntactic divergence between fluent and disfluent speech, the models aim to maintain parsing consistency across both types of utterances. The key innovation of our approach lies in the integration of repair-aware rules and the synchronization of parser behavior with the incremental nature of speech production and correction. Unlike many previous models that treat all syntactic structures uniformly, we systematically vary how the parser accounts for the interaction between the reparandum and the repair. To evaluate the effectiveness of these models, we conduct a comprehensive set of experiments using a well-annotated corpus of disfluent speech. Our results demonstrate that the proposed models achieve significant improvements over baseline approaches in parsing accuracy and robustness, particularly in handling utterance-final self-repairs and correcting segmented structures. Moreover, the models provide a more principled way to model the temporal and structural dynamics of speech disfluency, which is essential for developing speech processing systems that can handle real-world, conversational data.

Language models play a critical role in a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including speech recognition, machine translation, and text generation. A key requirement for real-world applications is robustness across diverse domains, where a model trained on specialized data may be expected to perform well on unrelated or unseen data. However, conventional language models often struggle in out-of-domain settings due to the limited contextual and distributional coverage of their training data. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a novel approach—hierarchical latent word language models (h-LWLMs)—designed to enhance the robustness and generalization capabilities of language modeling. Traditional word-based language models often assume that words are independent of their broader linguistic and contextual properties. While such models can achieve high accuracy within well-defined domains, they are prone to performance degradation when applied to out-of-domain or low-resource scenarios. Recent advances, such as latent word language models (LWLMs), aim to address this limitation by introducing latent variables that capture unobserved linguistic features or context in addition to the observed word sequences. These latent variables help to model variations and generalize better in unseen environments. Despite these improvements, existing LWLMs are still limited in their ability to capture multi-level or hierarchical linguistic phenomena. In particular, they tend to treat latent variables as flat and unstructured, which may not adequately represent the complex relationships between words at different levels of abstraction (e.g., morphological, syntactic, or semantic). To overcome this limitation, we propose h-LWLMs, a generalization of standard LWLMs that incorporate a hierarchical latent variable structure. This hierarchical framework allows the model to consider multiple layers of latent representations, enabling it to flexibly encode contextual information, latent linguistic patterns, and domain-invariant properties that are not explicitly present in the training data. The design of h-LWLMs is inspired by the hierarchical architectures commonly used in generative and representational learning. In this model, the lower-level latent variables capture local linguistic dependencies and surface variation, while the upper-level ones encode high-level patterns such as domain-invariant semantics or broader discourse structures. The hierarchical latent space provides a flexible representation that adapts to both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks. To facilitate scalability and practical implementation, we introduce a training method based on layer-wise inference, which decouples the learning process of lower- and higher-level latent variables. Additionally, we apply an approximation technique to manage the computational cost of latent variable inference in large-scale datasets.

Surface realisation is a key task in natural language generation (NLG), where a system takes a semantic or syntactic representation as input and generates fluent and well-formed surface text. In more complex grammatical systems, such as German, a variety of surface realisations can often express the same meaning—differing in word order, case marking, and syntactic passive/active voice. These alternations present both an opportunity and a challenge for data-driven surface realisation systems, which must learn to rank and select the most appropriate realisation from a large candidate set. This paper explores the use of underspecification in the input representations as a strategy to enhance the performance of surface realisation, particularly when predicting voice—whether a sentence is rendered in active or passive voice. Our work is situated within the context of a large-scale surface realisation system trained using a reversible grammar of German. We extend and evaluate this system by incorporating syntactic variants of both active and passive constructions into the candidate set, enabling us to study the interplay between voice and word order under realistic, corpus-based conditions. A central question driving this work is how the degree of lexical and syntactic underspecification in the input affects the system’s ability to recover the correct surface structure, particularly with respect to choosing the original voice of the target sentence. Contrary to fully elaborated inputs—which may constrain the model's generalisation ability—we hypothesise that appropriately underspecified inputs act as a form of linguistic scaffolding, enabling the model to better generalise over syntactic variations while leveraging the inherent richness of the grammar and training data. We present a novel approach in which a syntactic realisation model is trained to regenerate a surface string from a semantic representation, with the aim of predicting and reproducing the correct voice as it appears in the original text. Through this setup, we evaluate the model's ability to rank different realisation candidates and select the one that aligns with the target data. Our experiments are conducted on a real-world German corpus, using a data-driven ranking framework that incorporates linguistic knowledge encoded in grammar rules. The results demonstrate that by using underspecified inputs, the model achieves an impressive accuracy of 91.5% in predicting the original voice, significantly outperforming the baseline accuracy of 82.5%. This paper contributes to the growing body of research on data-driven surface realisation by demonstrating that the character of the input—specifically its degree of underspecification—plays a crucial role in the system’s performance.

Chinese word segmentation is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), especially for languages like Chinese that lack explicit word delimiters. It involves the identification of sequences of characters that form meaningful words within a sentence. This task is inherently challenging due to the vast number of possible word combinations and the coexistence of well-established and newly coined words in Chinese texts. Conventional word segmentation systems primarily rely on existing dictionaries and statistical models to identify word boundaries efficiently. However, such systems often struggle with the segmentation of new or rare words, a problem refer to as new word detection. Integrating word segmentation with new word detection is crucial for processing open-domain or rapidly evolving text corpora, such as social media content, news articles, or technical documents, which often contain many infrequent or novel lexical items. While traditional discriminative models, such as conditional random fields (CRFs), maximum entropy models, and support vector machines, have demonstrated reasonable success in Chinese word segmentation by incorporating rich contextual features, they still face significant computational challenges when incorporating high-dimensional feature sets in joint modeling. This becomes particularly apparent when we introduce new features tailored for the joint modeling of word segmentation and new word detection. Feature-rich models, which include word-based features capturing the impacts of known words and enriched edge features (i.e., label-transition features) modeling the coherence between adjacent segmentation decisions, have been shown to improve the performance of segmentation systems. However, these new features considerably increase the computational complexity of the training process. For example, the number of parameters to be estimated grows non-linearly with the number of features, and standard batch training methods become infeasible when dealing with large-scale datasets. This bottleneck severely limits the practical deployment of joint modeling systems in real-world applications. To overcome these difficulties and enable efficient training of joint segmentation and new word detection models, we propose an adaptive online gradient descent method that takes the frequency of different features into account. Our method assigns different learning rates to different features based on their occurrence frequencies, allowing the model to quickly converge on common patterns in the data while still learning less frequent but essential patterns effectively. By leveraging the sparsity and frequency distribution of high-dimensional features during the online updates, our training method significantly reduces the time required to converge to an optimal solution. The proposed learning algorithm is designed with scalability in mind and can process large-scale datasets with high computational efficiency.

Semi-supervised text classification is a crucial task in natural language processing, especially in scenarios where labeled data is scarce or costly to obtain, but unlabeled data is abundant. The goal is to build accurate classifiers by combining a small set of labeled examples with a large pool of unlabeled data. This problem is particularly challenging in deep learning contexts due to the model’s dependence on large volumes of high-quality training data to generalize well. Classic self-training and co-training approaches have demonstrated effectiveness but often suffer from error propagation, where noisy pseudo-labels from unreliable predictions are transferred to the model and affect the overall performance. Recent advances in semi-supervised learning within deep learning have introduced methods such as consistency regularization, mean teacher models, and pseudo-labeling, which aim to leverage unlabeled data effectively. However, these methods often treat the generative and discriminative components of the model separately, thereby missing opportunities to jointly and strategically improve the learning process. In this paper, we propose a   deep hybrid model   trained using a novel online fine-tuning algorithm that integrates both a   bottom-up generative learning pass   and a   top-down discriminative adjustment pass  . This approach introduces a hybrid architecture combining the advantages of discriminative and generative learning in a controlled, iterative framework. During the early stage of training, the model uses an unsupervised reconstruction loss to learn data representations from the unlabeled text, effectively forming a robust latent structure. Subsequently, these representations are refined in a top-down fashion during the fine-tuning phase through the use of the labeled data and pseudo-labels derived from the unlabeled instances. The proposed method ensures that the model not only learns a good representation of the data but also sharpens its decision boundaries using a carefully calibrated supervised and pseudo-supervised loss. Crucially, the   Bottom-Up-Top-Down (BU-TD)   algorithm allows the model to dynamically adjust its parameters in response to new unlabeled data points as they are encountered during the online learning process. At each step, the model first performs a generative processing step that captures high-quality latent features based on the input distribution (bottom-up), followed by a discriminative step that updates the classifier parameters based on both true labels and pseudo-labels (top-down). The integration of these two mechanisms enables the model to more effectively exploit the underlying structure of the text data, avoid error propagation, and maintain stable learning dynamics even with imbalanced or noisy pseudo-labels.

Topic modeling is a key technique in natural language processing and machine learning for uncovering hidden thematic structure in large collections of text. The advent of large and continuously growing text corpora, such as social media, news, and web data, has necessitated scalable inference algorithms to extract coherent topic representations in an online fashion. Online topic modeling relies on stochastic variational inference (SVI) to incrementally approximate posterior distributions of topic models over streaming data. This enables the analysis of massive datasets with limited computational resources and memory, making it an attractive solution for real-time or near-real-time applications. A critical aspect of successful online optimization in topic modeling is the learning rate schedule used during the gradient update step. One of the most popular adaptive learning rate methods is ADAGRAD (Adaptive Gradient Algorithm), which dynamically adjusts the learning rate for each parameter based on the historical sum of squared gradients. By scaling the learning rate inversely with the square root of the accumulated gradient magnitude, ADAGRAD prioritizes infrequently updated parameters and has shown strong performance in a wide range of convex and non-convex optimization settings, including deep learning and natural language processing tasks. Due to its efficiency and strong empirical performance, ADAGRAD is widely adopted as the default optimization method in many machine learning libraries and tools. Despite its popularity, ADAGRAD is not well-suited for online topic modeling, and this combination often leads to suboptimal convergence and unsatisfactory topic quality. In this paper, we explore the underlying reasons for this incompatibility and provide empirical and theoretical evidence to support our claim that the principles behind ADAGRAD work at odds with the requirements of online topic modeling. We show that one of the main culprits is the mechanism by which ADAGRAD normalizes learning rates using the square root of the accumulated squared gradients. In the context of topic modeling, the parameter updates are driven by gradients that are often large and noisy due to the sparsity of word co-occurrence statistics and the unbounded nature of topic proportions. As a result, the denominator in ADAGRAD's update rule becomes dominated by large values early in the training process, leading to an aggressive shrinking of the learning rate long before the parameters have fully converged to good estimates. This early reduction of learning rates has two major consequences for online topic modeling: first, it limits the model's ability to explore the parameter space adequately and capture nuanced topic structures early in the inference process.

The task of relation classification is central to a wide array of natural language processing (NLP) applications, ranging from information extraction to question answering and knowledge graph construction. The goal is to identify and classify semantic relationships between specific entities in a given sentence, such as “performed by” in “ John   wrote a novel ” or “located in” in “ The library is in  New York .” Traditionally, this task has been approached using feature-based or kernel-based models that rely on handcrafted linguistic information. However, in recent years, deep neural network architectures have demonstrated significant improvements in accuracy when applied to relation classification. These models can automatically learn complex, hierarchical representations of the input data, often surpassing the performance of traditional models without the need for explicit feature engineering. Despite these promising results, the evaluation of neural architectures for relation classification has been fragmented, with individual studies often testing only a single or a limited number of datasets. This narrow focus raises questions about the generalizability and adaptability of these models across different domains and language phenomena. For instance, a model that performs well on a dataset containing formal news articles may fail dramatically when applied to informal text, such as social media or speech transcripts. This shortcoming not only undermines the utility of the models in practical applications but also limits the insights we can gain into their strengths and limitations from the experimental results. In this paper, we aim to address these limitations by presenting the first large-scale, systematic evaluation of deep learning models for relation classification across six widely varying benchmark datasets. By covering domains that include both formal and informal text, as well as diverse syntactic and semantic characteristics, our analysis contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the architectural choices that lead to robust and generalizable performance. Central to our approach is a novel neural model we refer to as the “Man for All Seasons” architecture, consisting of a multi-channel LSTM combined with a CNN module. This design is intended to capture both the sequential and compositional aspects of sentence structure, while also incorporating linguistic features that have been shown to be important for relation classification. We evaluate our model on the aforementioned datasets and demonstrate that it achieves state-of-the-art results on two of them. However, beyond the quantitative evaluation, our primary contribution lies in the insights gained from the comparative analysis of different architectures.

Answering factoid questions using knowledge bases (KBs) has gained extensive attention in recent years due to its potential for real-time question answering in intelligent assistants, virtual agents, and semantic search systems. Two widely used benchmark datasets in this domain are   WebQuestions   (Berant et al., 2013) and   SimpleQuestions   (Bordes et al., 2014). Both datasets primarily consist of "simple" questions that can be resolved by following a single semantic relation in a knowledge graph (KG). For instance, a question like  "What city is the capital of France?"  can be addressed using the relation `capitals_of` to retrieve the correct entity  Paris . However, as the name suggests, these datasets do not test the system's capability on   complex  ,   multi-constraint   questions—those requiring multiple relations and entities to infer the correct answer. An example of such a question might be  "Which German actor died at the age of 80 and has won an Oscar for a science fiction movie?" , necessitating the intersection of multiple constraints, such as nationality, death age, film award, and genre. This limitation hampers the evaluation of knowledge-based question answering (KBQA) systems on real-world tasks, where the complexity and ambiguity of questions often demand a composite reasoning approach. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new benchmark dataset called   ComplexQuestions  , designed to evaluate the performance of KBQA systems on multi-constraint questions. This dataset includes thousands of real-world questions curated from existing QA platforms and verified manually, each requiring at least two distinct KB relations to compute the final answer. In addition to enabling more rigorous system evaluation, ComplexQuestions also serve as a valuable resource for training and improving robust reasoning mechanisms in KBQA systems. Beyond data collection, we propose a   constraint-based KBQA approach   to effectively address multi-constraint questions. Our method is built around the idea of progressively decomposing and translating the semantic components of a question into a set of logical constraints over the knowledge graph. To achieve high precision and recall, we incorporate techniques for relation mapping, entity disambiguation, and compositional constraint satisfaction. Our approach is modular, scalable, and flexible, and can be adapted to different knowledge graph schemas with minimal effort. It operates by first identifying the main entities and relations involved in the question, then systematically combining these into a filtering pipeline that incrementally refines the set of candidate entities until a minimal set (ideally one) of correct answers is found.

The semantics of verbs is a central topic in linguistics, cognitive science, and artificial intelligence. Verbs encode the core of eventive meaning in natural language, often expressing actions, events, and processes, and their meanings are structured by a variety of semantic components. Lexical semantics, particularly in computational applications, has long-standing goals of capturing and representing these semantic distinctions in structured forms that both reflect human understanding and support deeper language processing tasks. To this end, verb lexicons such as VerbNet have been developed, aiming to provide a comprehensive inventory of English verbs organized by their syntactic and semantic classes. However, despite their theoretical underpinnings and syntactic coverage, prior efforts in semantic representation within these resources have been limited in the availability of large-scale empirical validation and crowd-sourced data, which are increasingly being recognized as essential for robust linguistic modeling. VerbNet is an extensive, linguistically motivated verb lexicon containing approximately 6300 English verbs, organized into semantic-syntactic classes. It has been widely used in computational applications, ranging from semantic parsing and discourse modeling to machine translation and question answering. One of the key theoretical innovations of VerbNet is its system of semantic predicates—minimal conceptual elements used to describe the meaning of verbs. These predicates act as semantic primitives, and by combining them in compositionally meaningful ways, it becomes possible to model the complex meaning structure of verbs. For example, the verb  spray  is classified in the Spray class and semantically captures the event of an AGENT causing a THEME (e.g., liquid) that was originally  NOT  at a target LOCATION to now be in that location. This decomposition is grounded in cognitive notions of action and change, offering a formalized interpretation of real-world events through conceptual structure. While the VerbNet framework provides a theoretically rich and coherent system for verb classes and their semantic primitives, the empirical validation of these decompositions remains underdeveloped. Existing predicates lack extensive agreement or validation data across lay or expert populations, and the process of generating them often relies on internal linguistic intuition rather than systematic human judgment. As a result, the external validity of VerbNet's semantic decomposition system is an open question, especially in the context of tasks such as cross-linguistic alignment, affective semantics extraction, and deep semantic inference, where mismatch between formalized semantics and actual human interpretations can severely hinder performance. To address the need for more robust empirical testing of VerbNet's semantic predicates, we introduce the VerbCorner Project—a research initiative designed to assess and validate the current system of semantic decompositions via crowdsourced human judgment tasks.

Grammar is a central aspect of language comprehension and production, and its correct usage plays a significant role in academic, professional, and personal communication. With the growing reliance on technology to support language learning and writing assistance, grammatical error detection (GED) systems have emerged as essential tools. These systems aim to identify and correct grammatical errors in student writing or non-native language outputs, providing real-time feedback to aid writers in improving their linguistic fluency. Despite the increasing popularity and application of GED systems in educational and technological domains, the field faces significant challenges in evaluating their effectiveness. Evaluations are not only essential for comparing the performance of different systems but also for guiding the development of more accurate and reliable solutions. However, unlike many other NLP tasks, GED poses unique and complex evaluation challenges that are often underappreciated and left inadequately addressed in the literature. One fundamental difficulty in evaluating GED systems lies in the nature of the task itself, which is inherently multi-faceted and context-sensitive. A system must not only detect the presence of an error but also determine its type, scope, and the correct alternative to the erroneous construction. Furthermore, the evaluation of such systems involves reconciling three distinct entities: the writer’s original sentence, the annotator’s annotated correction, and the system’s proposed corrections. Each of these may differ significantly due to varying linguistic interpretations, ambiguity in the annotator's choices, or evolving linguistic standards. As a result, traditional evaluation frameworks designed for binary or sequence prediction tasks—such as those used in Named Entity Recognition or sentiment analysis—are often ill-suited for GED. They may fail to account for the richness of the error landscape and the complexity of the linguistic phenomena involved. Another critical issue in evaluating GED systems is the high imbalance in the data distribution, particularly the significant skew towards non-errors. In most linguistic corpora, such as those used for GED tasks like COIN and JFLEG, the number of error-free segments is vastly greater than the number of error-containing segments. This imbalance leads to misleading performance metrics such as high accuracy that do not reflect a system’s true ability to detect rare but critical errors. Standard metrics like precision, recall, and F1 measure are also affected, especially as they are computed without distinguishing the system’s treatment of high-stakes errors versus minor non-errors.

Speech recognition systems have made substantial progress thanks to advances in acoustic modeling and large-scale training data. However, even the most advanced systems face a persistent and critical challenge: out-of-vocabulary (OOV) word recognition. Traditional speech recognition systems are typically built using a closed vocabulary composed of a finite set of word units. While these systems can achieve high accuracy on in-vocabulary words, they are unable to process words that are not in their lexicon. These OOV words often include named entities (such as organizations, locations, or people), rare technical terms, or foreign language terms, which carry essential and often context-specific information, especially in domains like broadcast news, lectures, or technical discourse. This limitation is particularly problematic in open vocabulary speech recognition settings, where the speech system is expected to handle an unbounded set of possible words. One promising approach to alleviate this problem is the use of sub-word units: acoustic or phonetic segments smaller than complete words, often overlapping sequences of phonemes, syllables, or other sublexical forms. By modeling these sub-word units, the system can generate new, unseen words as combinations of known sub-components, thereby directly addressing the vocabulary coverage issue. Hybrid word/sub-word systems—combining traditional word-based models with sub-word units—have emerged as a viable solution. These systems augment the standard lexicon by adding a set of sub-word units derived from the phonetic or morphological structure of known words. Previous approaches to defining sub-word units have typically relied on heuristic methods, such as identifying frequent subsequences of phones using simple statistical criteria, which may not be aligned with the specific characteristics of the speech recognition task or the acoustic properties of the target domain. As a result, the sub-word units can be suboptimal in terms of both coverage and modeling efficiency. In this paper, we propose a novel probabilistic model for the learning of sub-word units optimized for a given task. Our method goes beyond heuristic data-driven approaches by explicitly modeling the problem as a joint acoustic and language modeling task. We aim to learn a sub-word lexicon that maximizes the likelihood of the observed speech data while enabling robust recognition of OOV words. The learned units are tailored to the target domain, such as broadcast news or academic lectures, which allows the system to better capture the phonetic and linguistic properties of the specific vocabulary that tends to occur in these settings.

Morphological analysis is a foundational task in computational linguistics, enabling a wide range of downstream NLP applications, such as machine translation, text normalization, and syntactic parsing. It involves decomposing words into their elemental morphs, categorizing their grammatical features (such as tense, number, gender, and case), and identifying their base or lemma forms. While supervised morphological tagging and lemmatization have seen widespread success in well-resourced languages, the majority of the world's 7000+ languages lack annotated corpora, making unsupervised and cross-linguistic approaches indispensable for low-resource scenarios. Traditionally, unsupervised morphological analysis has relied on probabilistic and information-theoretic models, such as Minimum Description Length (MDL) criteria, which aim to capture general properties of surface forms and their structure, independent of labeled data. A central assumption of these approaches is the encoding of task- and language-agnostic inductive biases, such as productivity of morphological patterns and regularity of inflectional processes. While such methods have been quite successful, particularly for agglutinative languages, they often struggle with irregular and partially productive patterns and are unable to exploit typological knowledge that could inform the discovery process. In this work, we shift the perspective on unsupervised morphological analysis by framing it as a structured prediction problem. Unlike traditional methodologies that seek to isolate universal linguistic priors, we treat morphological analysis as the task of transferring knowledge from richly annotated languages to unlabeled ones. Our core intuition lies in the principles of structured nearest neighbor prediction — the idea that a language's morphological structure is likely to resemble that of a semantically or typologically related language. To operationalize this, we define a universal morphological feature space, in which both labeled and unlabeled languages are embedded based on their observed word forms and inferred morphological configurations. Our approach avoids the need for parallel corpora or explicit cross-linguistic alignment, both of which are typically difficult to obtain. Instead, it requires high-quality labeled data for a set of source languages and minimal input for any target language (lexicons or raw text). The key innovation lies in a novel structured nearest neighbor learning framework that searches for a morphological analysis of an unlabeled language which is maximally similar in the feature space to a set of training languages with known morphology. To evaluate the efficacy of our method, we apply it to a set of eight inflecting languages spanning a range of morphological complexity. The results demonstrate that our approach outperforms a state-of-the-art MDL-based method on nominal morphology tasks, consistently achieving higher accuracy in feature tagging and lemmatization.

The task of sentiment classification has been a central focus in natural language processing (NLP) due to its wide-ranging applications in areas like opinion mining, customer feedback analysis, and social media monitoring. Traditional approaches to sentiment analysis heavily rely on domain-specific annotated resources, such as lexicons, rules, and labeled corpora. However, such resources are often scarce or imbalanced across languages, especially for low-resource languages. This poses a major limitation for efficiently developing sentiment classification systems in under-resourced languages. Cross-language sentiment classification (CLSC) was introduced to address this issue by leveraging rich, labeled data from a source language to build or enhance models for a target language. The core idea is to transfer knowledge across languages, typically from a well-resourced language like English to a resource-poor language such as Chinese or others. While significant research has investigated CLSC, the success of such approaches heavily depends on the ability to bridge the semantic and syntactic differences between the source and target languages. Bilingual word embeddings have emerged as a powerful tool in cross-lingual NLP tasks by learning distributed word representations that align the vector spaces of two languages. These embeddings help reduce the semantic gap, allowing for direct translation of word-level information between languages. However, as insightfully noted in prior work, conventional bilingual embeddings often neglect the sentiment component of language. Sentiment, being subjective and context-dependent, does not always map precisely through standard semantic alignment, making the application of these embeddings suboptimal for CLSC. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a novel framework for learning   Bilingual Sentiment Word Embeddings (BSWE)  . The BSWE model explicitly integrates sentiment information into bilingual embeddings, enabling the capture of cross-lingual sentiment patterns and improving their utility for sentiment classification tasks. The key innovation lies in leveraging small-scale labeled source corpora along with their translations in the target language, allowing our model to be trained without the need for large-scale parallel corpora, which are typically expensive and time-consuming to compile. By injecting sentiment knowledge into the bilingual representation learning process, BSWE enhances the discriminative power of the embeddings for both languages, particularly in low-resource settings. The embeddings not only align the semantic structure between English and Chinese but also encode the sentiment polarity of words, ensuring nuanced understanding and transfer of sentiment clues across languages. We evaluate our approach on the widely used NLP&CC 2013

Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing, aiming to identify and classify entities in text such as names of people, organizations, locations, and more. Despite its broad application, NER systems often exhibit a significant degradation in performance when applied to new or unseen domains. This domain adaptation challenge is primarily due to the shift in data distributions between source and target domains, where entity types and their contextual representations vary drastically. For instance, a medical transcription might heavily use terms like "cardiology" or "diagnosis," while a news article might feature terms like "election" or "government." Such domain-specific variations complicate the generalization of NER models without adaptation. The traditional approach to domain adaptation typically involves the use of labeled target domain data for model tuning. However, acquiring such annotated data is labor-intensive and often impractical, especially when dealing with multiple or rapidly evolving domains. This limitation has motivated research into unsupervised or semi-supervised domain adaptation techniques that require minimal or no labeled target domain data. Current methods in this space often rely on shared latent representations or transfer learning to bridge the domain gap, but they may fall short in capturing the nuanced contextual semantics that are crucial for NER accuracy across different distributions. In this paper, we propose a novel domain adaptation framework called Latent Semantic Association (LaSA) for NER. Our approach addresses the limitations of existing methodologies by explicitly modeling latent semantic associations between words, allowing the system to adapt to the target domain using only unlabeled data. The LaSA model leverages context snippets extracted from an unlabeled corpus to group words into semantic concept clusters. This enables the model to identify a shared concept space that abstracts domain-specific variations and facilitates better alignment between the source and target term spaces. Specifically, the domain adaptation process comprises two key steps: (1) mapping the term spaces of the source and target domains into a shared concept space using the LaSA model, and (2) refining the original NER model using semantic association features extracted from this concept space. By leveraging semantic associations rather than surface-level features, the model can better generalize to new domains, even when the distribution of entities and their context is significantly different from the source. We conduct experiments on both English and Chinese corpora to evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed LaSA-based domain adaptation approach. Our results demonstrate statistically significant improvements in NER performance across a range of domain shifts compared to various existing methods, including baseline and transfer learning approaches.

Recent advancements in automated essay scoring (AES) have led to increasing interest in evaluating student writing across a variety of linguistic and rhetorical dimensions. While much attention has been given to dimensions such as grammar, coherence, and content relevance, one particularly important but under-researched aspect of essay quality is  thesis clarity . The thesis statement is a central component of academic and argumentative writing, providing both the writer and the reader with a clear focus and indication of the paper’s intent. A well-formulated thesis helps organize the structure of the essay and enables meaningful evaluation of the argument. Conversely, ambiguity or lack of clarity in the thesis can undercut the coherence and persuasive power of the entire essay. Despite its importance, prior work on automated essay scoring has largely neglected the ability to model and assess thesis clarity systematically. While some early AES systems developed rich surface-level features to detect syntactic and lexical patterns, these methods often failed to capture evaluative aspects of argument quality, including thesis articulation. The task of modeling thesis clarity is particularly challenging due to its multifaceted nature: it involves understanding the discourse structure, evaluating the specificity and arguability of the thesis, and checking that the thesis is clearly expressed, all of which require deep linguistic and rhetorical analysis. In this paper, we address this gap by introducing a new annotated corpus centered on essay scoring for the thesis clarity dimension. Our corpus includes student essays from a range of academic levels, annotated along with detailed judgments indicating the clarity of the thesis. Alongside the dataset, we propose a learning-based method for scoring essays automatically on this dimension. Our approach is built upon a combination of features derived from syntactic structure, semantic similarity, and discourse cues that are relevant to thesis articulation. In addition to scoring, we consider the equally important problem of feedback generation. A valuable feedback mechanism can help writers understand why their essay scores the way it does and how to improve it. To this end, we introduce a second learning-based method that identifies the types of issues—such as ambiguity, vagueness, over-broad claims, or lack of arguability—that may contribute to a low thesis clarity score. These error classifications provide actionable insights, enabling accurate and pedagogically useful feedback to students. We evaluate our models on the proposed corpus and compare their performance against baseline approaches and human annotator agreement.

Multilingual neural machine translation (MNMT) is an important direction in modern machine translation research. The goal of MNMT is to build a single model capable of translating between multiple source and target languages, thus avoiding the need to maintain a separate model for every language pair. This not only reduces the computational and storage costs but also promotes cross-lingual generalization by leveraging shared linguistic representations across languages. Achieving this goal depends on designing models that efficiently balance the reuse of general information across languages with the ability to specialize for language-specific characteristics. Sequence-to-sequence models with attention mechanisms have become the standard for neural machine translation due to their ability to model long-range dependencies between source and target sequences . In the multilingual setting, the challenge is to share as many model parameters across language pairs as possible while preserving the flexibility necessary to capture the structure specific to each language pair. One common approach is to share encoder and decoder parameters across languages while using language identification tokens to disambiguate the input and output languages. However, while such approaches can lead to effective baselines, they often fall short in capturing the subtle differences between language pairs that are critical for high-quality translation. A key component of the sequence-to-sequence architecture is the attention mechanism, which determines how information from the source is used to generate the translation in the target language. Standard attention computes a weighted sum over all source tokens relative to the current target token, with the same attention mechanism used across all language pairs. While this promotes parameter sharing and consistency, it may not be optimal for capturing the distinct translation patterns across different language pairs. For instance, the syntactic and morphological differences between a high-resource language pair like English-German and an out-of-distribution, low-resource or zero-shot language pair like English-Finnish might require different attention strategies. In this paper, we propose task-specific attention models as a simple but effective technique to address this limitation in multilingual neural machine translation. Our method retains the shared parameter structure of the encoder and decoder to maintain the benefits of cross-lingual generalization. However, we introduce specialized attention mechanisms tailored for individual language-pair tasks. These attention models are used to compute context vectors for the decoder based on the input from the encoder and the current task (language pair).

Name Entities (NEs) are a foundational component in many natural language processing (NLP) tasks, ranging from information extraction to question answering and machine translation. The traditional Named Entity Recognition (NER) task has typically been modeled as a categorization task applied to text data with a clear and structured format such as news articles. Over the past decade, however, there has been a growing interest in adapting NER systems to more challenging and dynamic sources, such as web queries and other forms of user-generated content. Unlike news articles, web queries exhibit a high degree of variability in syntax, semantics, and domain content. This makes the development of robust, generalizable NER systems particularly challenging, as they must adapt effectively to a wide range of out-of-domain inputs with minimal training data. One of the core problems in applying standard NER systems to out-of-domain text is the domain shift, which leads to a significant degradation in performance due to the mismatch in linguistic patterns, entity distributions, and syntactic structures between training and test data. Conventional approaches to cross-domain NER typically rely on domain adaptation techniques, such as adversarial training, feature augmentation, or transfer learning from high-resource domains. While these approaches have proven effective, they often require access to large amounts of in-domain data and assume strong domain similarity, which is not always feasible for low-resource or rapidly evolving domains like web queries. In this paper, we explore an innovative approach to cross-domain NER inspired by the idea of  piggyback learning , where we utilize the vast knowledge and heterogeneous context provided by search engines to enhance the robustness of NER in low-resource and domain-adaptation settings. Specifically, our method leverages the rich contextual information available via web search results by submitting a token (or a phrase) with its surrounding context into a search engine and then extracting analogous or similar contexts from the search results. These additional contexts are then used as auxiliary signals during the classification of the token as a named entity. The intuition behind this approach is that similar surface patterns across different domains can carry similar semantic implications, thereby enriching the model’s understanding of the token in a domain-robust manner. Our key novelty lies in the strategic use of search engines to source contextual data that complements the limited in-domain training data available for tasks like web query NER.

There has been a surge of interest in the study of emergent communication among AI agents, driven by the goal of understanding how language and meaning can arise in agent-based systems through interaction and learning. This research direction builds upon the foundational work in referential games, where agents are tasked with communicating about perceptual observations—typically visual scenes—in order to achieve a shared goal, often with the use of simple communication protocols and negotiated symbols (Lewis, 1969; Steels, 1995; Lazaridou et al., 2017). While most prior works have focused on analyzing the structure of the language generated (e.g., quantifying the size of the lexicon, the complexity of the grammar, or the compositional nature of the system), the representation of perceptual input—particularly visual input—by the agents has received relatively little attention. This paper shifts the focus to the visual representations that arise within an emergent communication system. We examine the referential game setup of Lazaridou et al. (2017), in which two agents—one speaker and one listener—interact in the continuous environment of Color-Shapes Watercolor images, aiming to exchange information about a specific image through a short, negotiated sequence of symbols. While early investigations in this setting have largely centered on the production and comprehension of language, our study zooms in on the representations the agents form of their shared visual input and how these representations evolve during the communication process. We find that the speaker and listener agents reliably develop visual representations that are highly aligned with each other, which suggests that they arrive at a shared perceptual grounding for the symbols they use. This alignment is a crucial precondition for meaningful communication, as it ensures that the symbols refer to similar conceptual constructs in both agents' internal models. However, we uncover an important limitation: despite the convergence of the agents' perceptual representations, these representations do not encode the fundamental conceptual properties that are necessary for the interpretation of the objects in the images—properties such as object category (e.g., shape or color), object boundaries, or spatial relationships. This result is surprising and concerning, as it suggests that even when agents manage to establish a shared language, their visual understanding of the world remains shallow or misaligned with the intended semantics of the symbols. Furthermore, it raises the question of whether the constructed language conflates perceptual similarity with conceptual meaning, or whether the lack of deep visual understanding could hinder the scalability or robustness of emergent communication in more complex scenarios.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a foundational task in natural language processing, aiming to identify and classify entities such as person names, locations, organizations, and temporal expressions from text. Over the years, NER systems have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of languages, often built upon large-scale annotated resources and language-specific features, such as gazetteers and morphological patterns. However, the reliance on monolingual resources limits the applicability of these systems to low-resource languages or settings where annotated data is scarce or entirely absent. In such environments, direct replication of high-resource NER models fails to account for the linguistic particularities of the target language and often results in poor generalization. This is especially true for language pairs involving typologically divergent languages where orthographic and morphological structures differ significantly. To address this limitation, research in transfer learning has explored the idea of leveraging universal linguistic features that are predictive of entity structure and function across languages, enabling cross-lingual adaptation with minimal or no target language supervision. This paper introduces a phonologically aware neural model for NER that leverages language-universal phonological representations of characters, combined with lexical embeddings, to achieve robust NER performance in both monolingual and cross-lingual low-resource settings. The key idea is that phonological properties—such as syllable structure, phoneme inventory, and stress patterns—are more invariant across languages than orthographical ones, making them effective featurizers for transfer learning. By encoding raw character sequences into phonological representations, the model abstracts away from language-specific writing conventions and focuses on linguistic patterns that are more likely to generalize. This phonological embedding strategy is combined with an attention mechanism to dynamically weigh the contribution of each character-level phonological feature to the entity class prediction at the word level. Our model excels in monolingual NER tasks where it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines using only a language-independent representation. More importantly, it demonstrates strong cross-lingual transfer performance when adapting to a target language with limited or no supervision. To evaluate the effectiveness of phonological representations and the proposed architecture, we conduct experiments across diverse language pairs and present empirical evidence showing that phonological character representations outperform their orthographic counterparts in 0-shot and low-data transfer settings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the integration of attention with phonological features significantly improves the statistical efficiency of the model, reducing the need for task-specific feature engineering in both source and target domains.

Recent advances in word representation learning have led to the widespread use of pre-trained word embeddings such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), which provide dense vector representations of words by leveraging the distributional hypothesis. These approaches typically learn word embeddings by training on large corpora using either a skip-gram or continuous bag-of-words (CBOW) model, with the goal of preserving semantic and syntactic relationships among words. While such general-purpose embeddings have shown promising performance across a wide range of natural language processing tasks, they often underperform on domain-specific or task-specific applications, where the relevant linguistic patterns may differ from those found in general web text. To address the limitations of generic word representations, several recent approaches have proposed learning task-specific word embeddings via domain adaptation or fine-tuning. While these methods are effective, they often require careful hand-tuning of hyperparameters such as the learning order of training instances. This process is typically tedious and suboptimal, as it hides important, yet unexplored, aspects of how the lexical and semantic complexity of examples affects the representational quality of word embeddings. In particular, the order in which words or sentences are presented during training can significantly impact learning dynamics: complex examples may confuse early stages of training, while simpler examples may not provide enough challenge to yield rich representations. In this paper, we explore an alternative approach that treats the learning of word representations as a curriculum learning problem. Curriculum learning is a concept inspired by human learning, where training instances are introduced in an increasing order of difficulty. While this approach is intuitively appealing, the implementation of curriculum learning has historically relied on manually defined criteria for ordering training data, which may not be optimal across diverse tasks and domains. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel method that learns the curriculum automatically using Bayesian optimization (BO), a powerful framework for global optimization of expensive black-box functions. Our approach models the curriculum as a linear ranking function, which is parameterized by a weight vector. The weight vector is learned through Bayesian optimization by maximizing the performance of the target task that depends on the learned word representations. We define a feature vector for each training instance that captures various aspects of complexity, such as lexical diversity, syntactic structure, and contextual ambiguity. The scalar product of the weight vector and the feature vector provides a score that ranks the instances, from simplest to most complex.

Natural language processing (NLP) systems have achieved remarkable success in processing well-formed, standardized text across a wide range of languages. However, real-world text, especially user-generated content (UGC) such as social media posts, chat messages, and online forum discussions, often contains a variety of lexical and orthographic noises. These noises manifest in the form of typos, colloquial spellings, non-standard abbreviations, and variations in morphology and syntax. Such informal writing poses significant challenges to NLP tasks, including tokenization, part-of-speech (POS) tagging, syntactic parsing, and morphology disambiguation, especially in low-resource or morphologically complex languages. Dialectal Arabic presents a particularly complex setting for the deployment of NLP technologies. Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) serves as the standard written form of the language and benefits from extensive linguistic resources and annotation. In contrast, dialectal varieties such as Egyptian Arabic are used in daily spoken and informal writing and are marked by significant differences in vocabulary, morphology, and phonology compared to MSA. These dialectal variations, combined with the idiosyncrasies of UGC, lead to high degrees of data sparsity and ambiguity in morphological analysis. This in turn leads to reduced performance and high error rates for existing NLP tools that are primarily designed for MSA or formal data sources. Morphological disambiguation is a fundamental component in many Arabic NLP pipelines, providing critical linguistic features that support syntactic parsing, machine translation, and information retrieval tasks. However, the task becomes significantly more challenging in dialectal Arabic due to the lack of normalized spelling and the presence of code-switching, rare or hapax forms, and phonetic transcription errors. These difficulties are further compounded by the scarcity of annotated dialectal data suitable for training and evaluation. As a result, there is a pressing need for models capable of handling the unique characteristics of noisy dialectal text. In this paper, we present a neural network-based morphological tagging and disambiguation model tailored for Egyptian Arabic, one of the most widely used dialects in the Arabic-speaking world. Our model builds upon recent advances in contextualized neural representations and architectural innovations in sequence labeling, while introducing several novel components to enhance robustness in the face of noise and variation. Specifically, we incorporate character-level features, normalization modules, and multi-task learning to improve the system's tolerance for noisy input. Additionally, we explore the use of domain adaptation techniques and subword-based representations to address data sparsity in low-resource scenarios.

Sensory information is a core part of human perception and plays a crucial role in how we interpret and understand language. Everyday language is rich with expressions and terms that connote visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile experiences. For instance, when we hear a phrase like  the scent of fresh rain  or  the bright red of the autumn leaves , we automatically associate the words with specific sensory modalities. These associations are not only pivotal for our comprehension but also for the construction of metaphors, analogies, and emotional responses in language. This ability to intuitively link words to sensory experiences is embedded in our cognitive knowledge and underpins our interpretation of vivid descriptions, brand narratives, and literary works. However, the computational modeling of such sensorial relationships poses a significant challenge, as current natural language processing systems often lack the capability to recognize or process the sensory connotations of language. The development of a resource that systematically maps words to the five senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—could facilitate a wide range of language technologies, from sentiment analysis and content categorization to augmented reality and robotics. Imagine, for example, a system capable of rendering text into multisensory experiences, or one that can automatically tag a literary passage with sensory annotations to assist accessibility tools. Yet, despite the potential value of such a resource, little progress has been made in constructing a comprehensive sensorial lexicon. Existing lexical resources, such as WordNet or the ConceptNet knowledge graph, predominantly focus on semantic and syntactic relations, and rarely incorporate explicit sensory information, which limits their utility for tasks involving sensory interpretation. This paper presents  Sensicon , an automatically constructed sensorial lexicon specifically designed to associate English words with the five modalities of human perception.  Sensicon  is developed using a computational approach based on bootstrapping techniques and corpus statistics, eliminating the need for manual annotation or extensive human labor. The methodology is scalable and can be replicated for other languages, opening new avenues for cross-linguistic sensory analysis. The construction process leverages large-scale text corpora to extract frequent collocations and statistical patterns that indicate a strong association between words and sensory experiences. For instance, the word  jar  might be linked to the auditory modality due to its frequent co-occurrence with sounds like glass shattering or metal clinking, while  caramel  could emerge as goosmell due to its association with food or desserts. To ensure the quality and validity of the resource, we evaluate  Sensicon  against a gold standard manually annotated by human participants through a crowdsourcing task.

Sentence compression is a key task in natural language processing, aiming to shorten a sentence while retaining its essential meaning. This is especially useful in applications such as text summarization, machine reading, and document condensation. In previous work, neural network models, particularly those based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have demonstrated promising performance on sentence compression by learning deletions of words that are non-essential to the sentence’s primary message. However, one of the major challenges in applying such models is their limited ability to generalize across domains. When trained on data from one domain and tested on a different one, these models often experience a significant drop in performance, due to the lack of domain-specific patterns and syntactic knowledge in the learned representations. This paper investigates whether incorporating syntactic information can address this domain adaptation challenge and improve the robustness of LSTM-based sentence compression models in new domains. We propose two enhancements to the original LSTM-based model: (1) the integration of explicit syntactic features derived from constituent parsing, and (2) the inclusion of syntactic constraints through Integer Linear Programming (ILP) to enforce grammatical well-formedness of the compressed output. We hypothesize that syntactic information can serve as a stabilizing factor, allowing the model to maintain high performance even in previously unseen contexts. We conduct a thorough evaluation of our proposed model in a cross-domain setting. The results show that the incorporation of syntactic features and constraints significantly improves the performance of the original LSTM-based model. Moreover, our model outperforms a traditional rule-based sentence compression system that relies heavily on syntactic processing. This suggests that combining syntactic guidance with the powerful sequence modeling capabilities of LSTMs can lead to a more adaptable and reliable sentence compression framework. Our findings contribute to the broader research agenda in neural sequence modeling and domain adaptation. They indicate that while neural networks can learn high-level abstractions from data, they may still benefit from the inclusion of explicit structural information derived from syntax. This insight could be valuable for improving the domain robustness of other natural language processing tasks that involve sequence modeling. By demonstrating the practicality and effectiveness of a hybrid model that combines syntax with deep learning, we open up new possibilities for leveraging linguistic knowledge in neural architectures. Future work will explore whether similar improvements can be achieved through the incorporation of semantic or discourse-related features.

Temporal relation classification is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that aims to determine the temporal ordering or relation between two events or between an event and a time. This task is essential for applications such as event extraction, discourse understanding, and narrative modeling, all of which require a deep understanding of the temporal structure of text. The TimeBank corpus is one of the most widely used resources for temporal relation classification, providing annotations for temporal relations between a wide range of temporal expressions. While prior work has explored this task, most approaches have either simplified the original 14 temporal relations defined in the TimeBank into a more manageable, but coarser, set of six relations, or relied heavily on morphosyntactic features while underutilizing the rich semantic and discourse knowledge that could be mined from linguistic annotations. In this paper, we address the limitations of existing approaches by exploring a more fine-grained temporal classification paradigm. Rather than collapsing the original 14 temporal relations into six, we directly classify an event-event or event-time pair into one of the full set of 14 relations, preserving the discriminative power of the original classification schema. To enhance the interpretability and accuracy of our model, we incorporate sophisticated linguistic knowledge derived from a range of semantic features and discourse relations. For instance, we leverage features such as verb tense, aspect markers, and discourse connectives known to signal temporal coordination or contrast. Furthermore, we integrate discourse-based annotations, such as those from the Penn Discourse Treebank (PRD), to extract higher-level structural cues that can disambiguate complex temporal dependencies. Instead of relying solely on either rule-based or learning-based approaches, we present a novel hybrid architecture that combines the strengths of both paradigms. Rule-based systems offer transparency and the incorporation of domain-specific knowledge, but often struggle with generalization. On the other hand, learning-based models, particularly deep learning architectures, excel in capturing complex patterns from data but can be opaque and require substantial annotated examples for training. By combining a handcrafted set of rules grounded in linguistic insights with a neural network that learns from contextual patterns, our approach strikes a balance between generalization and accuracy. We conduct extensive experiments on the TimeBank corpus to evaluate our hybrid framework. The results show that our model achieves a 15-16% relative reduction in error over a state-of-the-art learning-based baseline.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for sequence-to-sequence modeling, offering a more end-to-end and potentially simpler approach to translation compared to traditional statistical machine translation methods.
